for leave to introduce Bill No. C-176, to amend the Criminal code (insanity at time of trial).

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT AND CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister going to make a brief statement?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT AND CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: EXTENSION OF MORATORIUM RESPECTING B.C. FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this legislation was originally introduced in 1959 and enacted because the statement of evidence submitted concerning the raw fish inquiry by the director of research and investigation cast doubt upon the legality of the arrangements and agreements between the fish packing companies and the fishermen relating to the supply
DEBATES	4729
Combines Investigation Act and price of raw fish. As a result the companies declined to negotiate prices with the fishermen's union as in past years and it appeared that a strike might result leading to the loss of the salmon catch and possibly other catches if legislation were not enacted to provide that the anti-combines legislation was not applicable to such an agreement during the period January 1, 1959 to December 31, 1960, both dates inclusive.
It has been necessary to amend this legislation from year to year by extending the period of its application as in the present bill. This extension has been occasioned by delay in completing the inquiry because of a series of court actions or injunctions bearing on the procedure in the inquiry.
In 1963 a federal-provincial committee of officials of the federal government and the provincial government of British Columbia was appointed, and they have now made a report. A recommendation of that committee is to the effect that negotiation procedures between the fishermen and the fish processors should be formalized.
It has not yet been possible to implement the conclusions of that federal-provincial report and it appears that, unless the exception is further extended and the exemption of the British Columbia fishing industry from the application of the act is continued, prejudice will ensue. Therefore the present bill provides for the extension of the exemption of the British Columbia fishing industry under the combines act and the Criminal Code.
It had been intended to ask for a further extension of 18 months, but in order to prevent the requirement of coming before parliament again in the event that the report is not implemented within 18 months the amendment has been drafted in such a way as to provide for a continuation of the exemption, it being provided, however, that the exemption will cease to be in effect if a motion of discontinuance is made and passed in this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, this is not such a simple and straightforward question as the President of the Privy Council has so blandly expressed it. It has a far deeper significance than explained by the hon. gentleman who introduced the bill.
To understand the significance of what I am about to say we need to look at the history. The statement of evidence by the director of research and investigation to
May 5, 1966

Combines Investigation Act which the minister referred arose out of a decision, as I understand it, of either six or seven people in the fishing industry who became disgruntled and unhappy because of a strike in the fishing industry a number of years ago. They took steps under the Combines Investigation Act to set out the basis of their claim that the act had been contravened and that a conspiracy to set prices had been engaged in between the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union, the Native Brotherhood of British Columbia, and the fishing industry of British Columbia.
The director of research and investigation under the Combines Investigation Act had no recourse whatever under the law but to launch an investigation, because the provisions of the law are that when six citizens of Canada lay a complaint together with background information before the director he is then duty bound to proceed to conduct an investigation. The director made a statement respecting the procedure itself, which became an issue in the 1957 federal election. At that time we argued, and we still argue, that section 4 of the Combines Investigation Act, which says that workmen or combinations of workmen may engage in activities for their own reasonable protection, should have been brought into force and that the investigation ought not to have been proceeded with.
The government of that day saw fit not to enforce the law, thereby protecting the rights of those in the fishing industry, but instead launched a prosecution. Subsequently there was a reluctance on the part of the fishing industry to negotiate with the fishermen's union over wages, hours and working conditions because it was claimed that if there were negotiations the companies in the fishing industry would be laying themselves open to another prosecution under the provisions of this act. Therefore, in order to ease the awkward situation prevailing in the fishing industry the original amendment was brought in exempting contracts, agreements and arrangements between fishermen or associations of fishermen in British Columbia from the workings of the Combines Investigation Act.
At that time we argued that the exemption ought to be permanent. We argued that if there was doubt in the minds of members of the government preceding this one as to the definition of "workman" in the fishing industry, which has been a perennial problem, that doubt ought to be resolved and some exemption should be provided for fishermen in the

fishing industry in British Columbia. We argued that the exemption should be a permanent one and should be brought within section 4 of the act which now provides a permanent exemption for workmen in regard to certain actions for which they would otherwise be prosecuted under the Combines Investigation Act.
I shall quote section 4 of that act so that it will appear on the record. It reads as follows:
Nothing in this Act shall be construed to apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees.
That section has been interpreted and reasoned to mean that a combination of workmen or a union that involves itself and a company or industry in collective bargaining for a collective agreement does not contravene the Combines Investigation Act by such negotiations in reaching a collective agreement. We say that this is the correct approach. There ought to be this protection and exemption from the conspiracy sections of the law in so far as unions and their collective bargaining rights are concerned. However, if there is doubt on the part of the government whether fishermen can be classified as workmen, then the provision in the bill now before us, which has been on the statute books since 1959, should be made permanent so as to extend to fishermen in the fishing industry of British Columbia or in any other part of Canada the same sort of protection that exists with respect to other workmen under the Combines Investigation Act. The present government and its predecessor have failed to make the exemption permanent. The failure to do so means that the government is engaging in the game of playing favourites. It is discriminating against a segment of industry for some peculiar or odd purpose.
In 1960 the Combines Investigation Act was amended quite extensively. We spent many hours, both in the house and in the Banking and Commerce Committee going over the proposed changes which were introduced by the hon. gentleman who is now the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) but who was then the minister of justice. One of the interesting changes made in 1960 was, in effect, a provision to exempt the fishing companies from prosecution under the Combines Investigation Act if they engaged in a conspiracy to fix prices in the export market. In other words, they were exempted from prosecution. The parliament of Canada in 1960 singled out one section of the industry under
May 5, 1966

what I called the Pickersgill-Fulton formula or amendment, because both hon. members conspired the one with the other, to develop the exempting section of the Combines Investigation Act which exempted that industry from prosecution under the act if it conspired to fix prices for the export market.
The effect of that provision in so far as the fishing industry in British Columbia was concerned was to bring about an exemption from prosecution for fixing prices in the domestic market. We all know that the various companies in the fishing industry of British Columbia, having been given the authority to sit down with each other and fix common prices for their products in the export market, surely do the same thing when they establish prices in the domestic market. Is there any suggestion that this does not happen? Certainly not. When we buy canned fish that comes from the coast of British Columbia we are buying canned fish whose price has been set by a conspiracy among the companies concerned which has the protection and sanction of law.
The previous government of that day, with the assistance and help of the present Minister of Transport, sought to exempt one section of the fishing industry in British Columbia from the law. This government has not the courage and the common decency now to take the next step, the one that ought to have been taken, namely, to exempt another section of the fishing industry from the provisions of the law. That is one-sided favouritism. It was one-sided favouritism when that concept was originally introduced. The President of the Privy Council is carrying on that one-sided favouritism by asking parliament to continue the temporary exemption respecting fishermen on the west coast. This is not nearly good enough.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It indicates that the President of the Privy Council has not learned very much as a result of his transfer from the position he used to hold in the cabinet to the one he holds now, that he has not come to appreciate that you cannot play favourites, that it is unethical to pick and choose among groups in the nation, that it is politically immoral to take steps to exempt the fishing industry from prosecution under the act while taking other steps to preserve the possibility that individual fishermen or their organizations may be prosecuted.

Combines Investigation Act
The gobbledegook of a while ago in explanation of the various safeguards was misleading, to say the least. There is only one reasonable, sensible, fair and just course to take. I can appreciate that the government may not fully understand what is meant by "just". But the only course which would be just to all so far as the fishing industry in British Columbia is concerned is this: If there is any doubt as to the interpretation of the word "workmen" or the phrase "combinations of workmen" in section 4 of the act we should take the bill now before us when we get into the committee stage and make this exemption permanent in the same way that a permanent exemption was granted to the company side of this industry.
The minister says that the bill provides for repeal because as soon as the collective bargaining procedures which may result from the work of the joint federal-provincial committee are worked out and in effect there will be no further need for exemption under the law. If a simple process of establishing a system of collective bargaining in the fishing industry of British Columbia will obviate the need to provide for an exemption from the law, what is the purpose of the law in the first place, because this system of collective bargaining is already in existence? What comes to mind is that there is in contemplation a collective bargaining procedure which will not be true collective bargaining but which will result in the imposition by one group of hours, wages and working conditions on another group. This is not free collective bargaining; it is dictatorship. If the minister contemplates the introduction of a system in British Columbia whereby one element in our society will be told what their hours, wages and working conditions shall be, I agree there could be no conspiracy because those who are under the heels of a dictator have a difficult time conspiring with one another.
One thing this bill has done has been to reveal once again the attitude of the present government which is identical with that of its predecessor and shows its complete lack of interest in fair play. It is not interested in fair play, only in paying attention to those elements in our society which have control of the government itself.

It is one which merits study because the fishermen and the fishing industry in British Columbia have been following certain practices since the last decade of the last century and nobody ever suggested that they were not legal until the investigation which took place in the late 50's.
Since the federal-provincial committee is now making a study of this situation, I think it is desirable that if ten members of the house wish to question the propriety of the exemption that right should be reserved to them. The result would be in effect that under this amendment the exemption for which the hon. member and others have asked in the past will continue in perpetuity, unless and until ten members decide they want to propose a change you will have a permanent exemption.

Mr. Speaker, I recognize that what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has just said is correct. Unless there is an objection made by ten or more members the provision will be permanent. What the minister neglected to mention is that there is a provision for the repeal of the bill as a result of other action by the house; in other words, if superseding legislation is brought in this measure may be repealed. That is my understanding of the position, and if it is not correct I hope the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) will tell me so.
I do not intend to speak at length on this matter but I should like to say that in my view it is nothing short of a national disgrace that for ten years uncertainty has hung over the heads of the fishermen of British Columbia. I was a member of the house when the complaint under the Combines Investigation Act was laid. It was startling at the time. It was even more startling to find that

the terms of the act which specifically exempt workmen were considered not to prevent the application of the section requiring the director to make an investigation. My impression was that the then minister of fisheries, Hon. James Sinclair, was as surprised as I was to find that this question had arisen in respect of a practice which, as the Minister of Labour has said, has been going on in British Columbia for decades, certainly for longer than I can remember.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I was not a member of the house at the time the action was taken to which the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) referred. I certainly agree it was a regrettable course of action but I shall not go into it. However, I would like to direct the attention of the house to the fact that in addition to that protective section in the Combines Investigation Act there are similar provisions in parallel sections of the Criminal Code.
I well remember the lengthy discussion which took place in the house during the 1953-54 session, when the Criminal Code was being completely revised, on this very question of conspiracy and the protection of working people from the application of the conspiracy sections of the Criminal Code. As we all know, the battle for the protection of working people against charges of criminal conspiracy goes a long way back into the history of our country and of that country where functions the mother of parliaments.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I consider it a national disgrace that this situation has gone on and on and that over the years there have been nothing but temporary extensions of the act. I do not know what kind of proposal will be placed before the house arising from the special committee of federal and provincial authorities, but from reading the committee's report I am not too optimistic that its proposal will be one that will really protect the rights of the fishermen of British Columbia. I hope I am wrong in my forecast.
Inasmuch as the hon. member for Skeena has referred to the section in the Combines Investigation Act I think I should put on record the parallel sections of the Criminal Code. Section 411 deals with the whole question of various types of conspiracy which might be considered in restraint of trade and commerce, including the fixing of prices. Subsection 3 reads as follows:
This section does not apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as workmen or employees.
May 5, 1966

Section 409 of the Criminal Code, also dealing with conspiracy in restraint of trade, says that such a conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to do or to procure to be done any unlawful act in restraint of trade. Subsection 2 states:
The purposes of a trade union are not, by reason only that they are in restraint of trade, unlawful within the meaning of subsection (1).
This, of course, raises the whole question of the determination of what is a trade union. The United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union has operated as a union on all fours with the normal operation of any other union in this country except that instead of bargaining on an hourly rate or monthly wage it has to bargain on a rate for piece work. But this is not a unique situation. The Minister of Labour knows that in relation to certain activities in the logging industry in B.C. the traditional method of bargaining has been on a price for 1,000 feet of lumber or logs.
No matter from which angle we look at this situation, for example, from the angle of this house having passed the Canada Labour (Standards) Code last year, it is incredible that even if we pass this bill we still leave unsettled the basic question of whether or not these fishermen are working people under the laws of Canada.
I am not going to prolong my remarks on the bill. Certainly I shall support its passage in lieu of any better proposal but I hope that the President of the Privy Council, who is perhaps not as fully acquainted with the circumstances surrounding this situation as the Minister of Labour, will take a good look at the definition of a workman around which this whole unhappy situation has hinged.

This clause, Mr. Chairman, carries with it a relatively new concept in legislation, namely, one which gives the initiative only in the repeal of a law and not its carrying out to any ten members of the House of Commons. I am in agreement with that general principle. It long has been my contention that the cabinet has taken unto itself far too much authority and control over parliament. At least in a small way the provision of the right to any ten members of parliament to initiate a certain legislative step is in itself good. The corollary of this, however, is that this right to take the initiative to repeal or remove the exemption applies only to fishermen in so far as the fishing industry is concerned. In other words, any time any ten members, for whatever reason, feel it is necessary to place the fishermen as individuals and their union in the position of facing potential prosecution for conspiracy under the Combines Investigation Act they can do so.
I think that what the President of the Privy Council should have done, if it is his sincere desire to see this procedure used, was not to have stopped here but rather to have given the same right to any ten members to
CMr. Favreau.]

initiate legislation to repeal the present sections of the Combines Investigation Act which permantly exempt the industry from prosecution for conspiracy to set prices. On the one hand he says that any ten members of parliament should have the right to remove the exemption which now applies to the fishermen, but on the other hand he says he does not want any ten members of parliament to have the right to remove the exemption which now applies to the company side of the fishing industry.
I submit that this is discrimination. As the law stands now, it says that the court shall not convict in any prosecution if there is a conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement relating only to the export of articles from Canada. As I pointed out, this is the argument that the fishing industry used as its defence for what the companies were doing in the period prior to 1956 when they came under the glare of the director of research and investigation.
They said then: We are not fixing prices on the domestic market; while it is true that we negotiate with the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union, in our selling policies we do not fix prices on the domestic market but, because of international competition, we have to be able to consult with each other to fix prices for the export market. I would point out that by a process which I believe Professor Skeoch called osmosis the price fixing arrangements on the export market also extend into the domestic market. And this is so.
If the minister is sincere in saying that any ten members of parliament should have the right to initiate a law to remove the exemption in so far as one section of the fishing industry is concerned, why did he not introduce a bill containing the same right to remove the exemption of the company side of the fishing industry as well? As the minister stated, this bill is a housekeeping measure designed to change the name and to make one or two other adjustments in the act. One of these adjustments is to relieve the National Research Council of its responsibilities in an advisory capacity or, to put it more accurately, to refer matters to

May 5, 1966
Research Council Act
a committee of the cabinet on science policy. I believe that in this principle a more coherent pattern is being followed than heretofore. I know from the minister's first statement that this results not only from the recommendations of Dr. Mackenzie, the past president of the National Research Council, but from studies carried out following his report. With the council on scientific matters and the secretariat in the cabinet we are beginning to get a framework now whereby we can separate policy and the investigational branch of the National Research Council's work into two parts under an over-all umbrella of a committee of the cabinet dealing with scientific matters.
My remarks today are directed through you, Mr. Speaker, not only to the National Research Council but to the minister who reports to parliament for it. Many people in Canada, over the last score of years ,have spoken at some length on the necessity of research as part of the adjustment that must be made in a modern industrial country in order to keep pace with technological advances. I should like to say, and I am sure the minister supports me in this, that the work of the National Research Council of Canada is outstanding the world over. My remarks are along the line that the tremendous effort by the National Research Council requires, I believe, a little reinforcement. Let me give some examples. One of the duties of the National Research Council is the job of doing basic research which might be classified, for the purpose of my argument, as government research. Within the field of government research a tremendous amount of pure research and applied research springing from pure research has been done. I do not believe that any country in the western world exceeds Canada in this regard.
With respect to the second duty listed in the act, whereby the National Research Council representing the government, if you will, joins with private industry to do research, there is much to be desired. The chief fact, as I see it, is that even though the relationship is voluntary between the National Research Council and industry there has not been as much government-industry research in Canada as there has been in most of the other industrial nations. I do not think this is the fault of the National Research Council to any extent whatsoever. As I see it, the fault lies in the fact that many industries in Canada are American owned or American controlled and they have developed a pattern

of behaviour under which their research is done for them by their parent companies in the United States. To a certain extent the remark I have just made about American owned and controlled industries also applies to British owned and controlled industries in Canada. In other words, the subsidiaries of foreign enterprises in Canada find it difficult, under the pattern of behaviour which has been established in their industries, to come voluntarily to the National Research Council and join with it in industrial research which would do so much for industry in Canada.
Therefore I am going to suggest to the minister, even though the act does not lay down any such responsibility for him, that he could serve his country well by using the considerable prestige which goes along with his portfolio in deliberately searching out opportunities where the facilities of the National Research Council could be combined with those of various industries which have the job of producing a particular product that is the end result of the pure and applied sciences in co-operative research programs. We do have some examples of this. In connection with nuclear development and the use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes in producing electricity, we have the example of the co-operation of the Canadian subsidiaries of Westinghouse and General Electric. The Atomic Energy Control Board has done tremendously fine work in providing us with a type of nuclear power production which equals anything in Great Britain or the United States.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In this particular type of co-operation these subsidiaries took great pride in the fact that they were able, in co-operation with a Canadian government agency, to go along a path different from that taken by the parent companies. They took great pride that in some aspects of this problem they exceeded the work done by the parent companies. I do not believe there was any loss financially to the parent companies; in fact, the opposite was the case.
I would suggest that the bringing together of these two subsidiaries of United States companies and a Canadian government agency resulted in benefit for Canada economically as well as from the point of view of prestige and research. I just use that as an example because I am sure there is need for the same thing in many other fields. I want to come back to this matter in a moment
May 5, 1966

Another phase of the work of the government research council is the contracting out and delegating of certain problems of research to the scientific departments of the various universities of Canada. One of the main purposes of this technique is to develop scientific facilities at our universities but at the same time to supplement the work of the National Research Council. It is this particular phase of the work of the National Research Council that I believe will enable the people of Canada, through the federal government, to bring about a tremendously increased amount of work which will not only add to our basic research but will be a device acceptable to the provinces which will allow the national government to play a large part in the financing of education in Canada.
I think the reports dealing with the cost of higher education indicate that the largest single component of that increased cost is and will be not only in the field of basic research but in the facilities which are made available to do this research. In this phase I believe the minister would have the support of all parties, including his own, if he were to use this as an opening wedge into the education field without in any way destroying the legitimate right of the provinces under the British North America Act to full control over education. This is an acceptable way in which we could move in this field.
This is something which cannot be pushed effectively by the personnel of the National Research Council; it has, I believe, to be a matter of deliberate government policy. I think that in this regard the minister will get not only the support of members of all parties but also the enthusiastic thanks of men and women across Canada who are trying to build up our higher levels of education.
I want to conclude my remarks on this aspect, Mr. Speaker, by reverting to the question of the minister's contribution in backing up, supporting and reinforcing the work of the National Research Council. I deal with this subject under the heading of "Education of the Public".
Let me turn, first of all, to education of industry. I do not think there are many of us here in the house who are not aware that through the basic research of government agencies we have produced new technology that should be utilized in our industries across Canada (a) to make them more competitive and (b) to produce new and superior products. Yet we realize that much of this basic knowledge, for the reasons I advanced 23033-301
Research Council Act
earlier, lies at the root of ownership and control.
I want to say without any malice whatever that I think I can put forward the thought that one of the functions of the minister as he surmounts the organization period in his department is more and more to make the country aware of what these technological changes are which have been made available by basic research here in Ottawa and across Canada. He should also publicize the fact that certain industries are not adopting these potential improvements.
I am not an expert in these matters, Mr. Speaker, and my views are only those of a layman, but let me once again give the house some tangible examples. I think of the mining industry. Canada is one of the leading mining countries of the world; yet the great bulk of the mining machinery utilized in Canada is imported from the United States. There has been a definite lack of basic research into the type of machinery required in our mining operations in Canada, and we actually build our mines around the type of machinery which is available.
The new move in Canada these last few years of beginning to re-examine the type of mining operations we are carrying on in this country provides a great oportunity to develop new types of machinery suitable to our own particular problems, which in turn could be put before the steel industry complex and the industrial machinery manufacturers in Canada. With the help of the National Research Council they could produce a type of mining machinery unique to Canada and which would be both efficient and suitable to the new type of mining I am now going to describe.
One of the new problems created by the new type of mining has resulted from the change from deep mining operations to the extraction of minerals from the surface-open pit mining, if you like. The type of machinery which is utilized in most cases is the same as that utilized for the extraction of any soil or dirt. Not enough thought has been given to the techniques of moving minerals or mineralized rock to the concentrator or to increasing efficiency to the point where there is a dramatic reduction in cost. I still see being used bulldozers and loaders that carry 12 to 15 tons and in some cases even 35 tons. The type of machinery used in building a highway is being used to move the rock to the place where it is crushed.

May 5, 1966
Research Council Act
There is also the type oi machinery which is used in the coal mines around Estevan in Saskatchewan. There the largest machinery in the world is used to move tremendous tonnages of coal per day per man, thereby producing a very low unit cost per ton. This is the type of machinery we must start developing in Canada not on a single unit, custom basis but on a mass production basis which would result in several hundred units every few years, thereby making available to open pit mining the type of low cost machinery which must be made available.
The reason I mention open pit mining is that much of the ore in Canada is low grade. To make money out of low-grade ore you first of all have to have a great volume of such ore and, second, you have to have a very low unit cost for moving the ore to the concentrators.
The Minister of Industry will be moving into a field already very large and lucrative, one which has already grown at a tremendous pace, and I have put forward this example so he will realize that here is a type of secondary industry which helps not only itself but primary industry to develop. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I am not an expert in this matter; these are the observations of a layman. However, I believe they merit examination by those around the minister who are experts.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
If there is merit in what I am saying I think the minister could serve his country well by bringing these problems to the attention of industry. The National Research Council could bring about a great forward step in the types of operations along the same lines as the steel industry which I should have liked to describe.
Most of us in Canada realize that for many decades to come steel will remain a basic industry of the modern industrial nation. We know that government agencies in Canada have done a great deal of work in this field. In that regard I should like to mention the metallurgical division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys which has done research work resulting in the addition of uranium to steel, thereby coming up with a steel the characteristics of which are superior to other types of steel being produced elsewhere in the world. Since we have the basic uranium supplies, since we probably have the largest iron ore reserves in the world, since we have the energy to process steel through electrolytic techniques, through the

traditional open hearth technique or through the new chemical techniques, and since we also have the water necessary to do this, a great advance in steel production can be accomplished.
As the United States rapidly becomes short of water for industrial purposes, which is probably more important than anything else, our water can probably be used as an inducement to bring heavy steel industry into Canada. If this is accompanied by increased technical know-how developed by our research people, with our basic energy, water and other resources I believe we can accelerate the fantastic growth of the steel industry even more than has occurred in the past eight years. Instead of being so proud that we have gone from 4 million tons to 8 million tons in eight years, let us think in terms of doubling and redoubling in short periods the present volume of 10 million tons.
In this particular industry we are completely competitive with the United States. As a matter of fact, we cannot even produce enough for our own needs in Canada, let alone export steel. I believe that the Minister of Industry could reinforce the work of the National Research Council if he were to inform himself as to what is available by way of know-how from the various government agencies, bring together all this knowledge and then ask pointed questions as to why it is not used. I will not deal with the other industries I have referred to in my notes. I have said enough to make my point.
My final point has to do with the consumer. In this field I know that traditionally the National Research Council has high ethics. When a product is produced by an industry and is brought to the National Research Council for examination, it is examined and the results are available if they are requested. Let me ask this question. How many times have the millions of home owners and consumers in Canada hoped and prayed for the day when there would be some form of easily available knowledge so that it would be possible to check on the efficiency and relative cost advantages or cost benefits of the various products available on the market? When a person buys a furnace, an automobile, a refrigerator and so on, he always asks himself when making his choice: What is the best article of that type for me?
I know that it is not according to the ethics of the National Research Council to issue comparative information of this type. But I have often wondered in thinking about the
May S. 1966

matter why the minister would not put himself in the place of the consumer today who is hard pressed by rising costs, not only of basic products but costs of distribution and those brought about by the tremendous added cost of advertising, and give the consumer some sort of standard to use from which to judge what is the best buy. Some sort of code might need to be set up. It might be part of the advertising; I do now know. I am simply saying that there is a tremendous need now among the consumers of Canada for some type of basic information that will enable them to judge what they are buying objectively in some reasonably fair way.
I know that when you buy an automobile you can get information from the automobile magazines published by private enterprise and thus get an evaluation that way. That is the sort of information needed when it comes to traditional hard goods such as stoves, refrigerators, dishwashers and all those things that go into a modern home, to say nothing of bigger things such as furnaces and so on.
I have made my point, Mr. Speaker, that the general principles of these housekeeping amendments have my support. Second, I have taken advantage of this opportunity, in the general freedom of the debate on second reading, to put forward some proposals that are additions to the terms of reference, if you like, to be utilized by the National Research Council. Most of the additional things I have suggested I hope will be given attention by the minister. I hope he will apply the dynamics of his position to achieve the ends I have suggested, because they really come under the understood terms of the act.
I am suggesting that the work of the National Research Council, plus the work of government agencies such as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the work done by research people in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Forestry and so on, should be brought together under the scientific committee of the cabinet. I think that the ministers on this committee, particularly the Minister of Industry, should take the tremendous amount of knowhow, the tremendous amount of basic information, and try to give to industry all the available knowledge in order to put Canada in a more competitive position, both as to cost structure and the variety and quality of new products, vis-a-vis other nations. I think we should all be very glad to support the minister in any initiatives he might take even

I think it is safe to say there will be no phenomenon which might be described as treading on the toes as between the Science Council and the National Research Council. As I pointed out at an earlier stage, though in the past it was the duty of the N.R.C. to formulate a science policy for Canada and to advise the Canadian government thereon, the council has tended over the years to preoccupy itself with somewhat more immediate and possibly more pressing questions such as the operation of substantial and effective laboratories and the granting of financial assistance in support of research in the universities as well as making strides along the road indicated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in encouraging scientific research and development within industry itself.
The National Research Council has not tended to address itself to the larger issues of determining scientific objectives for Canada as a whole and making some measurement of priorities. It is because the National Research Council has not been in the habit of doing this that Dr. Mackenzie recommended the setting up of a Science Council of Canada. The Science Council will be undertaking a task which the N.R.C. is not performing so its work will in no way conflict with the operations of the N.R.C. I fully share the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre of the excellent work which the N.R.C. has done in the past and which I hope it will continue to do.
So far as representation of the various government science agencies throughout Canada on the council is concerned, I would point out there are a considerable number of government departments and agencies, all of which are concerned with scientific research. If they were all to seek and be granted representation on the Science Council the latter would, I am sure, become an unwieldy body. We hope to have as members of the Science Council individuals who will be in a position adequately to represent the interests and the functions of government science.

Furthermore, provision is made in the Canada-United States agreement for a review late in 1967 of progress in achieving the aims and objectives of the agreement.
I have outlined somewhat briefly the measures which the government has introduced to enable the Canadian automotive industries, and particularly the parts makers, to adapt their production and their facilities to the new and expanded market conditions in an orderly manner. However, a major economic program of this nature is bound to require transitional adjustments for some workers and firms. For example, many parts makers are finding that the increased demand for their products means that they can only produce in sufficient volume if they substantially re-equip and expand their facilities. In numerous instances, whole new plants are required and are being provided. In order to ensure that no Canadian parts producer is prevented, by a lack of available financing, from modernizing or expanding his facilities in order to take full advantage of the opportunities afforded by the program, the government has established an adjustment assistance fund. This fund is administered by an adjustment assistance board under the chairmanship of Dean Vincent Bladen of the University of Toronto.
The board is authorized to make loans at an interest rate of 6 per cent and repayable over not more than 20 years for land and buildings and 10 years for other purposes. To date, 13 loans amounting to approximately $10.3 million have been made and a number of additional applications are being processed and under consideration.
Provision has also been made for transitional financial assistance to workers laid off from plants in Canada of manufacturers of motor vehicles or motor vehicles parts -because of the agreement. Because of the relatively buoyant market for skilled labour in the economy generally and in this industry in particular, only a small number of applications have been received for benefits under this program.

In summing up, I believe that the success of the automotive program is more than amply demonstrated by the new investments, the increased employment, the expanded production, the greater efficiency, the higher exports and the narrowing in the Canada-United States cost differential for vehicles. The program has brought new employment opportunities and greater prosperity for Canadians and has made a major contribution to the further development of secondary industry in Canada on an efficient and competitive basis. I therefore urge the house to give this resolution strong support and endor-sation.

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks the incorporation of a company

May 5, 1966
Private Bills
under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act to carry on business in all classes of insurance other than life insurance. The bill was introduced in the last session of parliament and was passed by the Senate on June 30, 1965, but received only first reading in the House of Commons before parliament adjourned.
The proposed company would be a subsidiary of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company of Hartford, Connecticut. The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company is a corporation carrying on a substantial general insurance business in the United States of America with its head office at Hartford, Connecticut. The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company, with its subsidiary, the Standard Fire Insurance Company, carries on business throughout the United States of America and in all classes of insurance for which application is being made in the bill to incorporate the Canadian Company.
The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company was incorporated in 1907 and operated as a partially owned subsidiary of Aetna Life Insurance Company until late in 1964, at which time a reorganization was effected under which all the shares of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company were transferred to and are now held by trustees for the shareholders of Aetna Life Insurance Company.
Aetna Life Insurance Company was incorporated and commenced to carry on business in 1853. It now carries on business throughout the United States of America and is one of the largest multiple line insurance organizations in the United States. Aetna Life Insurance Company commenced doing business in Canada over 100 years ago.
The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company of Hartford has conducted business in Canada for some years and has held a certificate of registry under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act for the past 47 years. A substantial part of the business conducted by the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company has been related to business conducted by the company with United States corporations having subsidiaries operating in Canada. A certain amount of direct business has also been carried out, especially in connection with major risks, an example of which is the liability insurance for Expo '67. The company has not maintained any offices in Canada but has carried on its Canadian business through agents, Dale and Company of Montreal.

Aetna Casualty and Surety Company has been reviewing its operations in Canada and has concluded that it would now be desirable that its direct Canadian business should be carried on by a Canadian company incorporated under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. It is felt that this step would enable the Canadian operations of the company to be developed more effectively and with greater Canadian participation in the conduct of the business.
It is proposed that the head office of the Canadian company, incorporation of which is proposed in Bill S-4, will be in Toronto. Because the scale of operations in the first instance will be small it is not proposed at the outset to establish a large staff, but the experience and the services of the Hartford company will be available for the assistance of the Canadian company.
The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company is convinced that the general insurance field in Canada is an expanding one in which a new Canadian company would have an opportunity to share without adversely affecting existing companies.
It is proposed that the new Canadian company will from the outset be prepared to undertake all classes of business. While the bill provides for a minimum paid in capital of $500,000 together with a contribution to surplus of at least $500,000 before the company commences business, it is the expectation of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company that in fact the paid in capital and contributed surplus will be in excess of these amounts before the company commences to carry on business.

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I express appreciation to the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron) for his fairly broad explanation which gives us a better understanding of the effect of the bill and of the company itself than might otherwise have been the case. I gather that in so far as writing insurance or participating in the insurance business is concerned, it really does not matter very much whether the bill passes because the company is in business through its United States parent and is writing insurance now. At least, that was the understanding I gained from the remarks of the hon. member for High Park.
The desire to incorporate a company in Canada under Canadian law permits of a bit of subterfuge and allows a company to capitalize on the psychology of Canadians who
May 5, 1966

like to see Canadian companies incorporated in Canada doing business in Canada. Yet in the over-all scheme of things the ownership and control of this company will not be here at all but in a foreign country.
Much was made some time ago of the provision in the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act which requires a majority of the directors of any company, and in the case of a company having more than one class of director, the ordinary directors or the shareholders' directors as the case may be, at all times to be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada.
Some of us advanced the reasoning in so far as companies other than insurance companies are concerned that this was thought at the time to be one way in which a company might think Canadian and act Canadian to a greater extent than might otherwise be the case. It was reasoned that if it was a requirement that the directors be Canadian citizens at all times ordinarily resident in Canada, this in itself would bring about a different psychology among the board of directors to the point that they would act, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) indicated a few days ago in his letter to foreign subsidiaries, as good Canadian corporations under the act.
If there is a desire to develop Canadian ownership and control of companies, to see companies operated in such a way that they are beneficial to Canadians first and foremost, then the mere requirement that the majority of the directors be Canadian citizens at all times ordinarily resident in Canada is not nearly sufficient. As we know, Mr. Speaker, money talks more powerfully than people, and in the field of insurance, as in other businesses, only scant recognition is given to international boundaries. The prime concern of these companies is the colour of the ink used to tally up the year's operations. Such being the case, the interest of companies like this one in things Canadian becomes secondary to their desire to be economical-I could say "efficient" by way of another euphemism-or, more properly, their desire is to conduct a profitable operation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am not persuaded too much by the argument that this company will be a Canadian company incorporated in Canada under Canadian law, with its head office in a Canadian city, or that this fact in itself will do much to augur well for Canada when the control of the company is in the hands of a group outside of Canada. It
Private Bills
also seems to me that this bill, seeking as it does to enable the company to write insurance from A to Z, which it does literally if one looks at the types of insurance in which the company wishes to engage-the whole alphabet has been exhausted in listing the various categories-should not be before us, because there is contained in it eight clauses which are spread over just a little more than one full page. The key part of the bill, the clause which carries the most weight, is clause 8 which states:
The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act shall apply to the Company.
The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act extends to some 111 pages in the booklet I have in my hand and contains innumerable sections going well beyond 150 in number. The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act is the controlling legislation here, not the bill now before us. All that the bill currently before the house does is to indicate that certain people desire to form a company. It gives the name of the company, the capital structure and the type of insurance the company wishes to write. I would submit, as I submitted earlier with respect to other bills, Mr. Speaker, that it is a much more desirable end not to have parliament waste its time considering the incorporation of such companies, and in saying that I make no disparaging remarks about this company. I simply say we have gone far beyond the point where this sort of business should be the business of parliament.
In this house we are concerned with public business. Every day someone or other makes the statement that parliament is wasting its time, that parliament is not getting down to public business. Yet the government, which has been reminded of this time and time again by myself, persists in clinging to this archaic system of forcing people who want to incorporate an insurance company to go through the parliamentary mill, to proceed through all of the tortuous processes in the other place, and simply in order to do business under a public statute, in this case the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act.
I have not looked too thoroughly at that act in so far as powers of incorporation are concerned, but presumably it is because of the terms of that act that Aetna Insurance, for example, and other companies of a similar nature have to come to parliament. I know this line of reasoning can perhaps be

May 5, 1966
Private Bills
looked upon as being outside the ambit of second reading of this particular bill.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
But it is a crucial and important point because the bill before us is one that is consuming the time of parliament. Whether it is examined scantily or in depth, it is consuming the time of parliament and of its staff because we are dealing with something which should not be here.
We have asked the government house leader to take steps by way of a public bill and bring in an omnibus piece of legislation which will permit groups such as Aetna Insurance Company to become incorporated in the same way as other companies, by going to a lawyer, asking him to do whatever is necessary and filing documents with the companies' branch to obtain letters patent to incorporate the company.
We think that is a much more sensible way to do things. There is relatively little interest in parliament whether Aetna Insurance Company is ever incorporated. Members of parliament have far more important things to consider. On their minds are matters concerning the very social structure of our nation and its economic well-being. They are the things parliament should deal with.
I should like to see this hour devoted to other kinds of business; whether it be government business, the introduction of public bills or the business of the public of Canada generally does not matter. I do not want to see the business of a few private individuals dealt with who are seeking to capitalize on the psychology that exists in Canada that a company incorporated by parliament somehow is better than one incorporated normally.
Whether the capitalization is $5 million or $50 million does not matter. Whether the shares are $50, $5 or 5 cents does not matter. I am sure it does not matter to the hon. member for High Park. It does not matter to members of our own party who will make up the initial board of directors. It does not matter what their names are, where they live or what are their occupations. Most of the other things in the bill do not matter very much either.
I submit that in this hour we should be seeking ways and means of preventing bills such as this coming before parliament. Public business generally ought to be dealt with. It does not matter whether it is an amendment to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act or something similar.

We do not require this tortuous process of incorporation for most other companies and I do not see why we should require it for insurance companies. Alternatively, we ought to require that all companies in Canada engaged in all sorts of business must be incorporated in this way. You cannot make fish of one and foul of the other. That, I submit, is grossly unfair.
I do not enjoy discussing Aetna Insurance Company. I do not enjoy the prospect that may be before the hon. member for High Park who in good faith is the sponsor of this company. I do not enjoy his having to proceed through this hour without his dream coming to realization, if that is what he wants. I do not enjoy the prospect of having to sit with other members in committee to go into the details of the operation of the company. I am sure there is not a solitary member in the house who enjoys such a prospect. I am sure all of us would much rather spend this period of time dealing with public business and not with the private business of those who want to enter the insurance field under Canadian law.
I hope that some day our words will carry weight with the government and especially with the Minister of Public Works as house leader. We hope he will see it is necessary to bring in a law providing for companies such as this to be incorporated in the same way as other companies.
We may have to persist in consuming the time in each private members' hour by talking on whatever bill happens to be before us. This is a regrettable course to take but we know from experience that often it is the only way to get action by this or any other government we have had in recent years. It is a course that has to be persisted in. We may be obstinate about it and sometimes incur disfavour and dislike among other hon. members who are affected in any way by the filibustering. However, that is not a prospect from which we shrink.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, this bill will receive second reading tonight and be referred to the appropriate committee. Perhaps it will not. In the long run it does not matter whether the bill passes. First, the company is in business and will still be in business and, second, one of these days the government is going to come to its senses and produce a general public law which will, I am sure, receive easy passage through parliament so that companies such as this one will not have to come to parliament in future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I certainly agree with my colleague the hon. member for Skeena that it is essentially a waste of time for the parliament of Canada to deal with these insurance company bills and others like it, nevertheless it does give me an opportunity to discuss something which will be quite in order and which has disturbed me for some years since I came to Ottawa. I refer to the proliferation of insurance companies in this country. Never a session goes by but that we have a number of insurance company bills on the order paper. I note that there are five now including the one we are discussing today. I want to assure my clansman from High Park that it merely happens to be his bill on which I am going to hang my remarks.
I think it is very appropriate that at this time we are discussing this bill, which is to incorporate a branch plant, shall we say, of a United States corporation, within the context of the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to which such prominence was given in the newspapers this morning. The minister was dealing with some of the acute problems facing the Canadian economy. You will recall, sir, that he was emphasizing the necessity for taking steps to offset the ever-increasing United States ownership of the Canadian economy and suggested that in order to do this we must encourage the generation of Canadian capital in order that Canadian capital can be involved in the development of our country. In connection with this bill I would point out, as I did a moment ago, that we have a continual proliferation of new insurance companies. The point I want to stress is that in our modern economy one of the most important methods of pooling the savings of the Canadian people and carrying out the wish of the Minister of Finance with respect to the generation of Canadian capital is by means of insurance.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I have noticed that in spite of the fact that we have more and more insurance companies incorporated year after year, in spite of the great myth of competition which is supposed to be so beneficial, the cost of insurance does not appear to be down. If anything, it appears to be continually rising. In fact, in some fields, particularly in the field of car and accident insurance, the cost has risen at such a rate as to give rise to public protest across Canada.
Private Bills
I think the answer is not far to seek. Far from there being genuine competition which will bring down insurance rates to the public, all we have seen is an increase in overhead costs, all of which has to be borne by the policyholders, and the division and disintegration of the pools of savings which have become available to the insurance industry in this country.
It is obvious that when conditions exist such as exist in the insurance industry today, when, for instance, the mere renewal of a policy which would perhaps occupy the agent concerned for about 10 minutes nets him between 10 and 30 per cent of the face value of the policy, the more insurance companies we have the less chance there is to accumulate the capital which the Minister of Finance is suggesting is our major concern.
Particularly is this the case with regard to a company such as the one which the hon. member for High Park is seeking to have incorporated today. This is merely another branch plant operation. If it is established and if it is successful, it will constitute a further drain on the resources of Canada and render us less able to combat the growing concern which is disturbing so many Canadians, the ever-increasing sector of our economy which is falling into United States hands. It will add, as have all the recent developments in this area, to our balance of payments problem though in a minor way, I suppose, since I gather this company is not to be a very big one.
If we examine the history of existing insurance companies which are branch plants of United States corporations we find that a large proportion of the funds they have accumulated from the Canadian people are invested in the United States. And in cases where they are not incorporated Canadian companies a large share of the profits is funnelled to the United States, adding to our balance of payments problem.
I think it is time the government of Canada and the governments of the various provinces took a serious look at the insurance business and considered carefully whether the number of companies engaged in it should be allowed to grow without any serious check simply by getting an hon. member to sponsor a private bill on their behalf and hiring the necessary legal talent. All this, it seems to me, increases the cost of insurance to the Canadian people while, as I say, breaking up and disintegrating the pools of capital formed by the savings

May 5, 1966
Private Bills
of Canadians, funds which could be pooled under public auspices.
I can think of one particular type of insurance which it seems to me it is altogether improper to leave in the hands of private companies. It is, of course, a preposterous situation that any private corporation should be placed in a position where it can tell me whether or not I can drive a car on the roads of this country. This is what happens when we leave insurance in private hands. The same argument could be applied to a number of other insurance fields into which the company we are considering is proposing to enter. I suggest that insurance coverage could be provided much more cheaply and much more effectively under public auspices than under the auspices of the various insurance companies.
If year after year we allow new insurance companies to become incorporated, these companies will have to fight for their share of existing business. The hon. member for High Park tell us the volume of business is growing. Of course it is. Our population is growing and the incomes of our people are rising. But they are not rising at anything like the rate at which insurance companies are proliferating in this country and I suggest that the more lucrative this field becomes the more insurance companies will try to enter it. In order to survive they will have to keep premium rates high, higher than they are now, thus causing increasing hardship to the Canadian people.
The insurance business to my mind is one of the very weak spots in our economy from the viewpoint of its contribution to the welfare of the Canadian people. I have watched it over the years both in the house and in the committees which have dealt with this subject and I have had an uneasy feeling that what I have been observing was merely, shall I say, the barnacles attached to the economic barque. One might use an even better marine analogy and say these companies are something like the lampreys which I understand are destroying the edible fish in the Great Lakes-parasites on our economy.
These companies draw very large sums from the savings of the Canadian people and give very little in return. In fact, I think it would be almost impossible to find any area in which Canadian citizens can be sure of getting so little in return for the money they invest. And the more insurance companies we allow to be incorporated the less will be the

money Canadians will get in return for their contributions in the form of premiums.
I urge the government to take a serious look at what is going on in the insurance business in Canada today. If they do not already know these things, I suggest members opposite should walk along the main street of any sizeable city in Canada and they will find that every real estate office advertises itself as an agent for one or more insurance companies. They will find insurance agents by the score along any business street in the country.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
They are deriving a livelihood out of the savings of the Canadian people which, as our Minister of Finance has told us in very emphatic terms, must be made available for the development of our country if we are to escape the fate that he and his predecessor in office appear to see before us due to foreign ownership of our economy. So, as my colleague from Skeena says, it will not make any difference to the people presenting this bill whether or not the company is incorporated. They will go on doing this anyway.
However, I hope the government will realize it is going to hear something about this each time this sort of insurance bill comes before us until it is prepared to take a serious look at what is happening to the Canadian citizen when he seeks protection in the form of fire insurance, accident insurance and all the other types of insurance listed in this bill.

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join those who indicate concern at the increasing number of insurance companies being incorporated. It seems true, however, that only a few major companies are involved, the rest being ancillary, and it seems that the individual insurance agent acts for a large number of these companies on a fairly indiscriminate basis.
When I go to an insurance agent to buy insurance he usually looks in his drawer and pulls out a policy issued by a particular company, but it does not seem to matter to him which company it is. It is rather like the man who is owed a debt and who does not really object if he does not get paid so long as the debtor puts his bill in the hat when he is choosing which one to pay.
Insurance companies drain off a large amount of money from our nation and it is something over which the country has little control. The last budget pointed out that we should have more control of finance and the
May 5, 1966

distribution of finance for the development of our country.
Each year our order paper shows a large number of companies seeking incorporation, and it appears that there will be absolutely no value to the Canadian public if the Aetna Insurance company is incorporated. It is not going to do Canada one bit of good. It is not going to do one individual citizen one bit of good. Therefore its incorporation must be for the benefit of the people forming the company.
The list of things which the company proposes to do is lengthy but many of them will be of little concern to the average individual in Canada. The list is synonymous with those provided by most other companies of this type.
Insurance companies share in the risk that they underwrite. It is safe to say that this company will not hurt the situation in Canada but in my opinion it is not going to help it. I believe members of parliament should look at the matter from a Canadian point of view.
The sponsor of the bill should give us a reason for incorporating the company. In passing may I say I do not know why, under our parliamentary system, the same hon. member is willing to sponsor a number of these companies. It may be that they are divvied around and that his turn comes up oftener than any other hon. member. I presume he has no knowledge of the people applying for the incorporation although he may have spoken to them.
Of the names mentioned in the bill three are those of counsel. Therefore I presume they have no particular interest in the incorporation and that the main people involved are Albert Bruce Matthews, executive, and Melvin Kirkland Kenny, insurance executive. It is true that the company meets the requirement of the act to have $500,000 in their possession before starting operation, and this is to be divided into shares of $50 each. If this bill were going to establish a mutual benefit society covering a large number of people there would probably be some justification for it but I believe there is no justification for the establishment of this company.
I did not hear anything said by the sponsor of the bill and so I am not aware whether Aetna was a name chosen from a hat, but I suspect Aetna is the name of a company in the United States which will have an interest in this company and will provide the $500,000
Private Bills
immediately. If this company is to be an extension of Aetna Casualty of the United States or Aetna Life Insurance or the Aetna Sickness and Accident Insurance Company, with several of which I have had previous dealings, it will turn out to be a well financed and normally operated insurance company. Therefore it will meet some of the criteria.
However, this raises the problem mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) of keeping in Canada the money earned by these companies and preventing expenditures being made in the United States. We have a deficit with the United States because hundreds of similar companies are able to take a large amount of money out of Canada.
One stipulation made by our Department of Insurance is that insurance companies operating here must at all times retain sufficient money to cover current liabilities. Therefore I presume this company will retain enough money in Canada for that purpose.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
We are faced with many of these companies which are only extensions of existing companies. I suppose it is a little like the analogy I drew a few moments ago of the storekeeper who does not object to the person who owes him money putting his name in a hat and drawing to see whom he will pay on pay day. I suppose this happens in respect of insurance companies and many of these insurance companies perhaps think to themselves, if we have 100 companies the chances of the name of one of our subsidiaries coming up more often is quite possible. This may be one of the reasons this is done.
In this country we should face the matter of insurance fairly and squarely and demand a reasonable return on the money invested so that we will get a fair break in the insurance rates. I think it also is true, when an insurance agent reaches into a drawer in his office, that no matter what the name of the insurance company is on the policy he draws out, whether casualty insurance or some other kind the premium on the policy will be identical with the premium of almost every other company for the same kind of policy.
If I thought that was not correct, the next time I buy fire insurance or some other kind I would ask for a comparison of the rates, but I have discussed this matter with insurance agents and they say it really does not matter which insurance company they insure me with because there is a set price anyway and

May 5. 1966
Private Bills
it is so much a hundred based on the facilities provided in the area in which one lives.
There is a total monopoly in the insurance field. There is absolutely no competition in insurance. If you get automobile insurance from Aetna Casualty Company of Canada, it will cost exactly the same amount it would cost had you taken it out through Aetna Insurance, General Insurance Company, Aetna car insurance company, Aetna auto insurance company or whatever other companies these people may have. So there is no competition. There is no justifiable reason why we should create a large number of additional companies when no service is being provided.
I am not aware of how the Department of Insurance, acting under the federal statute which provided for its creation, interprets several of the clauses which are included in the Canadian and British insurance Companies Act. The act does say, however, in the preamble:
Whereas the insurance business transacted within and outside of Canada by companies incorporated by the parliament of Canada, and by the legislature of the late province of Canada, and within Canada by British insurance companies, constitutes an important factor in the international and interprovincial trade and commercial relations of Canada; and
Whereas it is contrary to the public interest that insurance companies which are unable to discharge their liabilities to policyholders in Canada as they become due, or are otherwise insolvent, should be permitted to carry on the business of insurance in Canada-
It goes on to state what protection is provided. I think it is interesting to note the section which says that the establishment of these insurance companies constitutes an important factor in international and interprovincial trade and commercial relations in Canada. I believe this is true.
Therefore when we incorporate this company or any other insurance companies without any knowledge of whether or not it is in the interests of Canada, whether it is serving an individual purpose or is creating the possibility of additional coverage to that provided already by hundreds and possibly thousands of companies in Canada, it seems to me to be a waste of our time unless we collect a sufficiently large fee so that lawyers will really feel it is to their advantage to pursue the incorporation of these companies.
The other side of the coin, of course, would be the benefit received by those who hold shares in these companies because of the large amount of money invested by them.

The day will come very shortly when many types of insurance being underwritten by this company will not be carried by private carriers at all. That will be the day when we eventually decide to cover some of these items, and I will refer to several of them. One would be automobile insurance, another aircraft insurance, another guarantee insurance which is underwriting insurance or insuring insurance; another would be marine insurance which is becoming increasingly important with the advent of power boats and the large amount of equipment being used in a recreational way throughout Canada, a fairly recent innovation.
Sickness insurance obviously is a type of insurance which the federal government is considering in its intention of providing sickness and accident insurance through a national plan for all Canadians. Then there is another one which should be of national significance and that is weather insurance, if it means what it says, insurance against weather. There are many factors which go into bringing about a change in weather including a recent innovation which has come to my attention in northern Ontario. If we are going to change the weather and establish a company to insure against this, I should think that the federal government has some responsibility to decide whether or not this is within the jurisdiction of a private insurance company or is a major field of insurance in which the government of Canada must interest itself.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there are fields in which the federal government will have to interest itself. I think it is an absolute fact that we probably are 50 years behind the times in establishing companies in the manner we do by private bills. As has been pointed out, I think this matter must be looked at. I believe some consideration will have to be given to the national good in the establishment of these companies, which we are not able to give in isolation concerning a particular case when we are not aware of the over-all situation which would come to the attention of the Department of Insurance.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, insurance is in the public domain in a number of ways, and not only in the hoodwinking of the Canadian public which takes place in the establishment of all these companies which really are not companies but are subsidiaries of other companies competing with themselves while at the same time establishing fixed firm prices on certain types of insurance. It must be in
May 5, 1966

our interest to know the intention and the reputation of the insurance companies involved with relation to the Department of Insurance. Surely we did not establish the Department of Insurance just for fun; surely there was a reason behind its establishment and the establishment of a superintendent of insurance who supervises insurance operations.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
These bills are introduced as privately sponsored bills without any recommendation from the superintendent of insurance. We are asked to make decisions without having the advantage of the knowledge of the people we have appointed to supervise activities in this very complex and complicated field.
Surely it will make little difference whether we pass this bill or not, because the Aetna Casualty Company will not have agents in Canada. There will be a head office in Toronto, probably because this is a requirement of the law, but that will only be a place where the executive will hang out. This company will just send out forms to brokerage and insurance agents asking them to fill them in. We are wasting our time and the time of a good number of people by debating this kind of a bill because the people of Canada would be much better advised to do business with insurance companies now existing in Canada. Anyone who becomes a shareholder of this proposed company will be contributing money to the United States parent company.
