Mr. Speaker, like some hon. members who have taken part in this discussion I find that I have some serious questions in my mind as to the advisability of giving approval to the incorporation of this proposed casualty company. I regret that I will not be able to advance my reasons for thinking this way to the same extent other hon. members have done because of the limited time available to me. However, in the time left at my disposal I should like to make one or two comments about my serious doubts.
Very often heated arguments have been reported in the press regarding the high cost of administering charity campaigns such as the Red Feather appeal. These articles have given consideration to the question of whether the overhead of these charitable activities is justified. If one compares the operating overhead of organizations such as the Red Feather campaign with the operating overhead of companies such as the one proposed for incorporation by the bill now before us, I am sure he would realize how great the disparity is between these two.
Because of that fact, one often wonders whether it is in the public interest to proliferate almost endlessly the number and variety of companies operating in various fields of insurance. It is my opinion that the business of insurance involves perhaps the most expensive bookkeeping system in this country. It is obvious that the insurance business is not productive because it does not create new wealth in our society. This is a business of keeping accounts and records. The way in which this proposed company will operate, similar to that of many other companies, is something which should give us cause for consideration, particularly when we are asked to increase the number of incorporated insurance companies in Canada. While I should like to pursue this debate, I will conclude my remarks on this stage.

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADA-U.S. AGREEMENT ON AUTOMOTIVE PRODUCTS

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Drury:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the agreement concerning automotive products between the government of Canada and the government of the United States of America, signed on January 16th, 1965, and that this house do approve the same.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADA-U.S. AGREEMENT ON AUTOMOTIVE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the commencement of private members' hour I just had time to outline the steps I propose to take in debating the resolution now before us. This is one of the most important matters to come before this house and it affects many people.
The Canada-U.S. automotive agreement has far-reaching effects and involves very complex and complicated matters. I only wish that in preparing my remarks, I had the battery of officials available to and at the minister's disposal. Because this is such a complex and difficult subject I can only speak as a humble layman, but I propose to bring to the attention of this house the facts that have been brought to my attention by some of the individuals engaged in the automotive industry in Canada.
The Canada-U.S. automotive agreement was entered into by the government after having been conceived in secrecy, born in mystery and developed in controversy. This is a free trade agreement which provides for free trade for the producer but not for the consumer.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
When you speak of free trade, you immediately think of free trade for the consumer as well as the producer. We must realize that the automotive industry in Canada was forgiven an amount of $50 million in the form of tariff reductions. This amount would have been collected from the industry if the treaty had not been instituted. I am broadminded enough to realize that this pact has its good points as well as its bad points. There are always two sides to any coin, and I am prepared to look at both sides. However, I believe that the present government in bringing this treaty into being had one major decision to make, and it was a political

decison. If anyone in this country is asked what is the main difference between the two predominant political parties in this country today, I suggest that this treaty would be an example one could use to illustrate that difference.
We in the Conservative party, practically since the days of its formation, have believed, since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, and we still believe, that if you sell the economic birthright of your country you at the same time lose your political birthright. In other words, if a company in the United States has 61 per cent of the shares of a company in Canada, I think we all realize who will control that company; it will be Uncle Sam, or the United States.
Therefore I think this was the first decision that should have been made by the Liberal government before entering into this treaty. They apparently believe that Canada can sell her economic birthright and still retain her political birthright. I am one of those who do not believe this. Time will tell whether we in this party are taking a short-term view of this very important matter of free trade in the car industry between Canada and the United States. Have we sold out, in the long-term view, our economic control of this industry, or is this just a short-term outlook? I am afraid we have sold out our economic birthright in this industry, and I believe we must be prepared to pay the consequences.
I am a little confused about the thinking of the Liberal government in regard to policy. Just last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) made a speech in Toronto. I should like to read a few quotations from the Globe and Mail of today's date regarding what he said concerning Canadian ownership of industry:
There is of course not only the question of the proper conduct in Canada of subsidiaries of foreign owned companies. I am even more interested in the retention and the establishment in Canada of Canadian-owned and controlled corporations.
Does this U.S.-Canada car treaty create a situation of which the Minister of Finance speaks? In my opinion it creates just the opposite situation. The Minister of Finance went on to say:
Canadians must strive to have their share of head offices. It is desirable too, that companies who have their major production facilities in Canada should have their head offices in Canada. Unless these views are accepted in the Canadian business community, we shall have to accept the limitations that go with a branch office economy.
May 5, 1966	COMMONS
Does not the United States-Canada car treaty create a branch office economy in this country? I humbly suggest that it does. In his speech the minister went on to say:
It is important too that we realize that there are certain key areas of our economy which must he controlled by Canadians.
Yet we sell out our car industry to the United States. Then he said:
As a final but by no means the least important item on my economic and financial "agenda for independence", I would put industrial development policy.
The minister went on to explain what he meant by that. Then he said:
If we are to be true nationalists today we must think in terms of a different kind of economic nationalism, which seeks to strengthen Canada in the context of growing interdependence between the nations and our obvious interest in the expansion and liberalization of world trade.
Having read that speech of the Minister of Finance, I cannot understand how he expects to have anything but a branch office economy in Canada flowing from this United States-Canada car treaty. We come back again to the old matter of cross-purpose legislation that seems to arise so often in the Liberal ranks.
In this regard I think of the last session of parliament when the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) was introducing this car treaty. It seemed to me he was suggesting a take-over of Canadian subsidiaries. At the same time the minister of finance of that time, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), was doing everything in his power to retain industry in Canada with Canadian control. It seems to me they were working at cross-purposes. Let us consider another field. The former minister of agriculture announced the payment of subsidies on the growing of tobacco, if this was necessary, and the former minister of national health and welfare spent $700,000 in asking people not to smoke cigarettes. This was cross-purpose legislation to the greatest degree.
Then we found the Department of Labour at cross-purposes with the Department of Justice. The former minister of labour announced the spending of a $3 million advertising program to get people 45 years of age back to work; yet the former minister of justice, when asked in the house about this situation, said, "No, we do not hire people over 45 years of age." One minister authorized the spending of $3 million to put people over 45 years of age to work, and another
DEBATES	4759
Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement minister would not hire them. Then we had the situation concerning cars of $5,000 in value imported from the United States. The former minister of finance did not want these cars imported, so he said, "All right; there will be no income tax depreciation allowed on these cars. We do not want them to come into Canada." Just about that time the Minister of Industry introduced the free trade car treaty. So again we had another piece of cross-purpose legislation. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it must be proven to me that the Minister of Finance is thinking along the same lines as the Minister of Industry in putting into operation this U.S-Canada car treaty.
Having said that in the form of an introduction, I should now like to deal with the objections we have to the introduction of this resolution. First is the manner in which this matter has been handled. How was it done? It was brought in by order in council; we never had an opportunity to debate it in the house. The Minister of Industry, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and another minister went to the United States and signed this treaty on President Johnson's ranch. Other officials went with them. On January 16 they announced to the people of Canada that they had entered into a far-reaching treaty that would be of great benefit to so many people in Canada. They did this without even giving elected members of parliament the opportunity to debate the matter or have anything to say about this very complicated treaty.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I ask, why was it done by order in council? Why was parliament not asked to endorse this before the treaty was signed? Before I leave that point, let me say that I cannot understand the change of thinking in the Liberal party since the days of their former great leader and prime minister, the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King. I quote here from a speech he made on June 21, 1926 when he was speaking in the House of Commons. Parliament was being asked to adopt a resolution standing in his name, the final paragraph of which read:
That the house considers that before His Majesty's Canadian ministers advice ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signifying acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
Those were the words of the late Mackenzie King. Then on April 12, 1928, in the
May 5, 1966

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement course of a debate on the international sanitary convention, the same right hon. gentleman had this to say:
I submit that the day has passed when any government or executive should feel that they should take it upon themselves without the approval of parliament, to commit a country to obligations involving any considerable financial outlays or active undertakings. In all cases where obligations of such a character are being assumed internationally, parliament itself should be assured of having the full right of approving what is done before binding commitments are made. I would not confine parliamentary approval only to those matters which involve military sanctions and the like. I feel that parliamentary approval should apply where there are involved matters of large expenditure or political considerations of a far reaching character.
This treaty certainly falls into that category. That was the thinking of the former leader of the party across the way, but apparently that is not the thinking of today. This treaty was signed, sealed and delivered without the elected members of parliament having an opportunity to voice their opinion one way or another.
What about the commonwealth? Since we are the senior member of the commonwealth, I believe that we should have had at least some respect or some thought about what effect this far reaching treaty would have on the commonwealth. As you know, cars are imported into Canada from the commonwealth free of duty. However the minute this treaty came into force American cars were allowed to come into Canada duty free. The English cars immediately had to meet this stiff competition, which was anything but fair.
What about GATT? We are supposed to be members of GATT, think highly of it and respect it. As all hon. members know, under the terms of GATT any member or nation which gives special privileges to any other member must give the same opportunity to all other members. I do not know whether this has been done or not. I do not think it has.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADA-U.S. AGREEMENT ON AUTOMOTIVE PRODUCTS
speechtext: It has.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADA-U.S. AGREEMENT ON AUTOMOTIVE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I sincerely hope it has. The minister has never told us whether it has or not. This treaty has been in force for 15 months. There are so many things we do not know about it. We have asked for debates and so on, but we have never had an opportunity to discuss this matter.
The second objection we would like to register in this regard is the delay in bringing

the matter before the house. As I have just stated, it is 15 months since the treaty was signed and we have had no chance whatsoever of debating it. A supply motion was used back in 1965 and this was the subject which was debated. We had a very limited opportunity to discuss the matter at that time. We have asked numerous questions from time to time, which is about the only opportunity we have had to learn more about this very complex and far reaching subject. As I have said, this is a subject of great complexity and certainly every opportunity should have been given to allow the members to look into the whole question.
Those are the objections I wished to raise under that heading. The next heading was, what were we told that this Canadian-United States car treaty would do for Canada? I believe I am quite reasonable and fair when I list these four points which the minister told the house would be the important and beneficial results from the treaty. First, he said it would increase employment substantially and, second, that it would correct the rising trend of imbalance of payments in the automotive industry. Then third, it was understood that it would enable the Canadian automotive parts manufacturing industry to achieve a lower level of costs which would be competitive with United States parts manufacturers producing similar parts. Fourth, it would help to equalize the Canadian factory costs and selling prices in the automotive industry with costs and prices in the United States. In other words, Canadians would be able to purchase cars at the same prices as are paid for American cars. These were his selling points for this treaty.
Now let us take a look at these points one by one. The first was to increase employment substantially. I know the minister, in his introductory remarks, said that 10,000 more people are employed in the industry today. However, I would suggest to him that he forgot to subtract from that figure those people who have been put out of work in the industry. I am thinking of car parts manufacturers who have found it necessary to close their plants, and in other cases to reduce their staff. I do not propose to dwell on this subject. I know one hon. member in our party has had a car parts manufacturing firm close in his riding, throwing hundreds of people out of work. In my own riding I have had a manufacturer of car electrical harnesses who has had to lay off approximately 30 people because he can no longer compete
May 5, 1966	COMMONS
with his American competitors in the manufacture of car harnesses. Then not only do we have these industries closing, but it also affects the associated industries.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I know that in Windsor they have benefited from employment in many respects; I would ask the minister and those who boast about the great increase in employment whether these are the types of jobs we really want to maintain in Canada. I would ask the minister for a list of the extra people who have been employed in skilled capacities, such as draftsmen, technologists, purchasing agents, and all the way down the line. I know for a fact that Ford closed their Oakville purchasing department and moved it to their head office in Dearborn, Michigan. The firm which closed in Beaverton was the Canadian subsidiary of a United States plant, and it closed its doors because parts could be made cheaper at the head plant in the United States, which parts they can now ship into Canada duty free. So that if you want to create a lot of jobs for people on the production line, people who put nuts and bolts, together you can do so with ease; but I would ask the minister to think about the skilled men and technologists in the trade as well.
I know for a fact that McKinnon Industries in St. Catharines who have been making steering gear boxes for Chevrolet cars, is closing down and moving operations to their United States plant. How will this create more jobs in Canada? I know that the In-gersoll Machine and Tool Company had to find another line of manufacturing, or close down, because they lost their gear box steering business with Chrysler of Canada. This goes on down through the industry. Car parts manufacturers are losing orders. They are getting by on their 1967 model bids, or some of them are, but others do not even get the opportunity to bid.
In some cases these people have had to go and cry on the minister's shoulder, and ask him to help get orders for 1967 models or else they would have to close their doors. Is this the kind of treaty we want, Mr. Speaker, with individuals sitting on the minister's doorstep asking him for business, and with the minister telephoning Chrysler, General Motors and Ford and telling them to see that these people are given business because he does not want them to close their doors?
With regard to the second point, that the minister said this treaty would correct the rising trend of imbalance of payments in the
DEBATES	4761
Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement automotive industry, how many times have we heard this said? How many times did the minister go across the country in October, campaigning for the November election, telling the public what a great thing the car treaty was and how it would improve our balance of payments? As a matter of fact, our balance of payments position today has deteriorated to the extent of $100 million compared with last year, despite what we were told. While we argued, as did the minister, that it would cut back Canada's automotive deficit, the true picture is that it has increased it nearly $100 million, resulting in an imbalance of trade between the United States and Canada, so far as the automotive industry is concerned, of $674 million.
I agree with the minister that Canada's exports to the United States more than doubled in 1965; I do not question that for a minute. The figures went from $76 million in 1964 to $164 million in 1965. But United States exports to Canada far outstripped Canada's exports to the United States-$184 million compared with $838 million. So the result for Canada was that the net automotive trade deficit with the United States rose from $578 million in 1964 to $674 million in 1965, an increase of $96 million.
It was shouted from the house tops that this treaty would help Canada's imbalance of trade position; but the true picture is that we are now $100 million further in the red than before the treaty came into effect. I will say no more on that point.
The third point was that it would enable the Canadian automotive parts industry to achieve a lower level of costs and make them competitive with United States parts manufacturers producing similar parts. What do we find in this regard? The minister had some very fine objectives in this field, but once again he forgot to talk to the Minister of Finance. Here again they are at cross-purposes in their legislation.
During the budget debate the Minister of Finance did not remove the 11 per cent sales tax on productive machinery. The Minister of Industry told the people engaged in the car parts industry to go ahead and instal machinery; that they would have to buy machinery in order to increase production and bring about an efficient operation. He even set up a fund from which they could borrow money to buy machinery at 6 per cent interest. He may not in so many words, have said the 11 per cent sales tax would be removed, but these people were led to believe that it would be removed.
May 5, 1966

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement
According to the Globe and Mail for March 31, 1966, the car parts manufacturers had this to say on this particular point:
Canadian auto parts manufacturers yesterday reacted angrily to Finance Minister Mitchell Sharp's failure to remove immediately Canada's 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery.
Parts industry spokesman said retention of the sales tax for the next year will impose such a heavy penalty that their companies will be unable to compete successfully-
A little later the article continues by stating that-
-his group's members were urged by Ottawa to buy the new equipment so they could produce parts in large enough quantities to serve the North American market. He said that because of Industry Minister C. M. Drury's encouragement, Canadian parts makers went ahead with expansion plans, although they felt at the time that the 11 per cent sales tax was a severe competitive handicap.
"We know that our U.S. competitors were not hampered by any comparable sales tax-
And so on. There is no 11 per cent tax on productive machinery in the United States, but there is in Canada, and the Canadian car parts manufacturer is supposed to compete with his United States counterpart. The article continues:
-but Mr. Drury told us to have the courage to expand" . . . Mr. Drury should have been talking to Mr. Sharp, not to me . . . When a government advocates free trade and then does something like this, you begin to wonder where the brains are!
So, on the one hand they talk of free trade; on the other hand they inhibit it or make it impossible for Canadian car manufacturers to compete. As I have said, in order to compete with the United States competitors, Canadian manufacturers have to buy machinery and produce efficiently. But first of all they are hamstrung with the 11 per cent sales tax on machinery. Then they cannot buy all this machinery in Canada owing to the backlog of orders and have to buy some machinery from the United States. They import it into Canada, making it subject to a customs duty of 22J per cent. Then they are told to go ahead and compete with their neighbour across the line and do the best they can. There is free trade on the one hand, and they are cut off on the other.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Another problem faced by the car parts manufacturers is opportunity to bid. I think the minister realizes, as I do, that the minute you cross the border into the United States there is only one way to get an order, and that is to offer the same or a lower price than that obtainable in the United States. They are

not going to buy from Canada if they can get it from their own producers in the United States. The only way they will buy here is if it costs less. The farther south you travel in the U.S.A. the more difficulty you have. You even have difficulty in getting your Canadian dollar accepted as exchange.
This brings up another point: Where would the car parts manufacturers of Canada be today if it were not for the 92J cent dollar that the Conservative government introduced a few years ago. The devaluation of the Canadian dollar has kept the Canadian car parts manufacturers in business. If it had not been for that, the whole bunch of them would have had a really difficult time, and more of them would have been out of business than are out of business today.
My time is running short, and I wish to bring up some other points. The point I wish to discuss is that it was claimed the Canadian people would be able to buy cars at reduced prices. The minister quoted prices this afternoon. He said that the main car manufacturers had reduced car prices. I am not going to dispute that. All I have to go on is what people have said to me who have bought cars. I have been told that they have had to pay the same prices for identical cars as they had to pay before the treaty came into operation. I have not purchased an automobile recently, and therefore I cannot speak from experience. However, people have written to me to say that they have found no difference whatsoever in identical cars bought this year, and those bought prior to the institution of the treaty.
I am told that 80 thousand cars, according to figures I have, made by Canadian Chrysler workers in Windsor, were shipped to the United States and each of them is sold for $615 less than the same model of car is sold for in Canada. Why cannot the same car be sold for the same price in Canada? Is the public in Canada subsidizing this company so as to allow it to sell cars more cheaply in the United States, or is that company making more profit on the cars it sells in Canada? Even taking into consideration the difference in the tax of 11 per cent, it still does not add up to $615. This is supposed to be a free trade treaty. I say that it is free trade for the producer but not for the consumer.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I go back to the points I mentioned at first. We object to the way in which this measure was introduced. We object to the failure of the government to
May 5, 1966	COMMONS
give the elected representatives an opportunity to debate this very complex legislation, and to deal with the points the minister said would be forthcoming by this treaty. I have tried to the best of my ability to show how some of these things, that were claimed would come about, have not come about.
Many people in the industry would like to have a say in this matter. I think this whole question ought to be sent to the Committee on Industry Research and Energy Development. People could be given the opportunity to appear before that committee, and lay their problems before it in addition to any ideas they may have concerning this unique but yet unproven treaty which was the idea of the Minister of Industry.
I conclude by saying what I said before: I am broadminded enough to know that there are some good points and that there are some bad points in this treaty. It remains to be seen whether there are more good points than bad points. I do not know how else we could find out, other than by calling people in the industry to appear before the committee and give their views. Failing that, time will supply the answer. In due time we shall know whether it was a good or a poor treaty.
I would remind the minister and I would remind his party that the first decision they should have made was a political decision and not an economic one. Their economic decisions, or principles, and our economic principles are not quite the same, because we feel that if you sell your economic birthright you lose your political birthright.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADA-U.S. AGREEMENT ON AUTOMOTIVE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in some ways we are engaged in a curious debate. The order paper says that we are to give approval to an agreement, or to an arrangement made by the Government of Canada some 15 months ago. It is a unique experience for us to have the infant before us 15 months later and to be asked to approve of his birth. Of course, what we are doing now is not legitimizing the infant, as my colleague behind me says, but reviewing the agreement and the changes which have taken place under it.
I was very interested in the remarks of the previous speaker, who seemed to feel that before the agreement was brought into effect the government ought to have decided whether or not we could have a Canadian automobile industry of our own. I would say to him that that decision was made many years ago. Canada, at least as far as the automobile
DEBATES	4763
Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement industry is concerned, passed the point of no return long ago. There does not now seem to be any way in which we can economically construct a Canadian car manufacturing industry. The decisions that brought this situation about were made many years ago, and are probably irreversible.
Of course, the agreement brings out the whole problem of foreign ownership. The real problem, it seems to me, about foreign ownership in Canada does not come out of trying to make political decisions. The real problem that I have encountered in the little travelling I have done in Canada is that the Canadian people themselves do not have the guts to build a Canadian owned economy. They want all the advantages and the high standard of living that comes with increasing domination by the people to the south, but they are not prepared, from what I have been able to ascertain, to make the effort and the sacrifice that would be involved if we were to try genuinely to come to grips with the whole problem of foreign control of our economy.
In the few minutes I have available I should like to deal with four aspects of the problem. What I say may be somewhat repetitious. I want first to deal with the general background, and with the way this whole agreement came into effect. Second, I want to touch on its general performance to date, in the light of the forecasts made for it by the minister. Third, I want to bring out some criticisms of the pact in certain areas where we feel it can be justifiably criticized, and where we think it needs strengthening, notably with respect to the prices of cars, assistance to displaced workers, and as it affects car part manufacturers.
In conclusion, and fourth, I want to make some general observations of what we think are certain disturbing aspects of the plan, which seem inconsistent with certain fiscal policies of the government and with its professed interest in the field of foreign control.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
It is interesting to look back and remember the circumstances in which this agreement came about. No doubt there was some need for an approach such as this, given the general picture of the automotive industry in Canada which, effectively, as has been pointed out, was a branch plant operation built up behind the protection of tariff walls. It has always had a limited manufacturing base- short runs resulting in higher prices, making it virtually impossible to get into export markets.
May 5, 1966

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement
Canadians would not be prepared to accept anything but a wide variety of models. We all look at those great Canadian programs, Bonanza, and the Dinah Shore show, which create in us a desire for all the models and ranges the Americans have. This has always resulted in a measure of inefficiency in production here. For example, in Oshawa, in the 1965 model year, 595 different types of cars and trucks were assembled, while the most complex assembly line in the United States was building 256 models. Hon. members can see the difficulty, or the danger, of this situation.
In order to cure this state of affairs, hon. gentlemen opposite introduced what is called the Drury plan. This was an arrangement for the remission of taxes. The minister will recall that it was brought in with all the fanfare which he is capable of bringing to his imaginative schemes. We on this side said we thought it looked suspiciously like an export subsidy, though we hoped it would not be so regarded. However, it was immediately regarded as being such and quickly ran into lots of trouble with United States tariff authorities. When it became obvious that the commission would find against it, some of the "whizz kids" in the Department of Industry got busy and drew up this plan to counteract what appeared to be the implications of the Drury plan. This is how the present pact came about.
The intent behind it is good and in some ways it is an imaginative solution to the problems of the industry. The intent is to rationalize and integrate the industry so that specialization can occur on both sides of the border. Let us hope that this will lead to increased expansion, more jobs, more efficient products, a lowering of prices opening exports to the U.S. market, and an easing of our balance of payments position.
As has been said, this is an important agreement. It was introduced in the usual Liberal fashion amid fog and secrecy, lack of information and midnight diplomacy. Then all concerned went down to Texas to sign it. Later they came back and told us what had been done. We were able to get very little information from the minister about this agreement but he did give us his bland assurance that all would be well because he was handling the affair. As a matter of fact we obtained most of our information from the hearings in Washington. Incidentally, it has always been embarrassing to me as a member of the House of Commons that we
have to rely on the senators in Washington to snap their fingers and get the detailed information which we wanted from our own government in Canada but could not get.
It seems to us that important policy changes of this nature involving taxation and finance should be given the full legislative treatment, rather than coming before the house later to be rubber-stamped or inadequately criticized by an unprepared and possibly inadequately informed opposition.
Contrast what is being done here with the way in which this was handled in the United States. The issue went before the legislative committees of both houses. Exhaustive investigations were made and full disclosure of information was obtained. Only afterwards did the legislators feel they could pass judgment. It seems to me we should follow this example to a far greater extent in Canada. While we may be in agreement as to general objectives, our inability to criticize important measures involving taxation and finance is, it seems to me, one of the reasons why our parliament is not giving effective leadership to the country. This is sensed by the public and it is partly because of this failing that our parliament is at a low ebb in terms of public esteem.
This leads me to the consideration of the general performance of the agreement. I listened with interest to the minister extolling the virtues of the pact. Nothing like it, he said, had ever happened before. What he says is, to some extent, true. The performance of the automotive industry generally has been phenomenal. There has been a notable increase in production and sales. For example, in 1961 production amounted to some 328,000 units. By 1965 the figure had jumped to more than 710,000. This is a remarkable increase. Sales rose from 446,000 to 786,000 in the same period, again an amazing performance for an industry.
I do not know what proportion of this increase is attributable to the agreement. I do not think the minister knows. Obviously the figure would be hard to establish. All the investigations we have carried out indicate that a good deal of this expansion would probably have taken place in the absence of an agreement. This good performance does not really tell us very much about the plan. A better test is to see what is happening to our balance of payments figures.
I can remember when the plan was introduced. The government made an extravagant

May 5, 1S66	COMMONS
presentation claiming that this was the answer to our whole balance of payments problem. This, they said, would cure it. Of course it has not done so. The imbalance rose from $386 million in 1961 to $615 million in 1965. This was the net deficit in the automotive industry. I realize that it might well have been worse in the absence of an agreement. Indeed I suspect this would have been the case. But the agreement has not been the cure, the answer, as we were all led to believe it would. I know the minister will tell us that the deficit is becoming less serious each year than would have been the case had there been no agreement. But this does not help us much, in view of the fact that it is continuing to increase. I should like the minister to tell us what he has in mind-what means he proposes to employ to deal with this problem since, to date, the agreement has not done so. I should add, however, that in other areas the agreement has been a real source of success. There has been increased production and there have been more jobs provided-and we are glad to see this happen.
I wish to turn, now, to the third section of my submission on this subject-the price people have to pay for their cars. We all remember the discussion which took place when we were told that the automotive companies would, in effect, receive a "bonanza", a saving of $50 million, because they would not be paying the tariff charges. We were told that a lot of this money would be passed on to the consumer. Any way, we were told, the poor automobile companies needed the money in order to finance their expansion programs. General Motors needs the money like we need three holes in our heads. It is coming out its ears. But we were told these poor companies needed this money for expansion purposes and that, anyway, they were going to pass it on to the consumers in lower prices.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
It is hard, because of the complexity of the situation, to give comparative prices of Canadian passenger cars and those of comparably equipped United States cars, but some attempts have been made. The minister himself made one in the Toronto Globe and Mail on October 14, 1965, when he said that the gap remaining between Canadian and U.S. prices, after the adjustments made in the price of 1966 cars in Canada, was about $150. This was done by taking a high volume model and comparing it with the U.S. counterpart. If you take smaller models it goes down to $100. If you take a model like the
23033-302J

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement Oldsmobile Delta it is $600, but anyway there is a substantial difference between the two.
Have the manufacturers passed these savings on to the buyer? My suggestion is that they have not, that they have engaged in a lovely piece of window dressing, in a fantastic financial double shuffle to try to convince the public that they are passing on these savings. If you take the $50 million that has in effect been handed to the companies and spread it over the 580,000 cars involved, you realize the average saving per car is about $86 to the companies. With the release of their 1966 model price lists last fall there was a great fanfare and the big three, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler, claimed reductions. I think General Motors said a reduction of $73, Ford claimed $62, and Chrysler did not provide a figure; but they all did it in the same way.
They compared the cost of 1966 models with the cost of 1965 models equipped with a safety package now included as standard equipment, and they said, "Because we are including this safety package and not increasing the price, the consumer is actually getting a very substantial reduction in price." But, Mr. Speaker, when they were examined on this in the United States they were forced to admit that producing all these safety features on an assembly line basis cost about $22.
This cost would be a little bit higher in Canada. We would accept the figure of perhaps $30 as the cost to the companies of producing this safety package on a production line basis as distinct from special gadgets. The companies reduced their prices by $3 or $4. They added in $23 worth of safety features, and it must be remembered that the average saving per car to the companies was $86. If you take off the little extras they have thrown in as safety features, then the car companies pocketed $50 on every car.
For example, the net effect of this to General Motors, which produces 300,000 cars a year, was that it pocketed $15 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money. It did not pass this money on. It kept it and stuck it in its profits. Its profits were so low that it needed this extra money. In 1965 General Motors had a profit of only $2.1 billion. Chrysler stroked along on a profit of $233 million. General Motors net profit in Canada averages around $59 million, which is second only to the Bell Telephone Company. The poor auto companies really had a rough time.

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement
This is one of our complaints, that the government is not assuming any responsibility or giving any leadership in the field of prices. To us it is imperative that it do so. It is pretty clear that normal growth will not be big enough to absorb the expanded output that the government has set for the motor industry, and unless car prices are reduced so that Canadian manufacturers can get into the United States market there will be further dislocation. We want the government to take some action to protect the consumer, to free the consumer and remove the wall of protection that has been built around this multimillion dollar industry.
If the companies are not prepared to reduce prices then there is a remedy, namely reduce the tariff that individuals pay. If Ford of Canada does not want to make cars available at a reasonable price, then people can drive down to Buffalo to buy new cars and have a real good week end on the money they save. People in Vancouver can go down to some other American city and buy their cars. This would be the quickest and the most effective way to force these autocratic car manufacturing companies into giving greater consideration to the Canadian consumer.
The third criticism we want to make deals with the transitional assistance. This was an arrangement called TAB, transitional assistance benefits, to compensate workers who were put out of work as a result of dislocations arising out of the auto pact. I can remember being in the house and listening to the then minister of labour and the Minister of Industry telling us what a magnificent plan this was going to be, and how the generous motor companies would rush in to make their payments to the government so that the workers would be eligible for assistance.
We asked the government if it did not think it a little unusual to have an arrangement whereby the motor companies had to participate voluntarily in return for the $50 million handout, and we were told no, that there would not be any difficulties, that General Motors, Ford and Chrysler were just waiting for the legislation to be passed so that they could run down to Ottawa and give the government a cheque for their contribution. Well, as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, none of them has made any contribution.
Out of 1,500 workers dislocated, not a dozen have received any help under the TAB plan. Because the companies did not voluntarily contribute, their workers are not eligible for the benefits. As a result, when out of

work, the workers have been forced to rely on the benefits provided by their collective agreement.
In its usual cheapskate fashion the government has forced the workers to carry the burden of a change in tariff policy, a tariff policy designed to protect and help the whole country and the economy generally. But the government has not assumed its responsibility. It has left it up to the workers. The collective agreements were designed to cover seasonal lay-offs. They were never intended to cover this tariff adjustment, and in the usual cheapskate way that this government does everything, it has let the workers carry the burden.
At the time it was introduced I asked who was paying the tab. Now the tab is being paid by the Canadian auto workers. The payment by the companies should be made mandatory. Subsection 5 of the regulations which provide for this sort of voluntary participation should be deleted because the workers are being rooked over this deal, and are being unfairly and improperly treated.
We would hope that some decision would be made by the government. I am not going into the whole problem, that our benefits are worse than the Americans are able to attain. Their benefits and wages are considerably superior to ours. This is something we have discussed with the minister on other occasions but he has indicated a blind eye, and so there is not much point in trying to do anything about it now.
The third objection has already been covered by the previous speaker, dealing with the problem of the car parts manufacturers. The 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery results in these people having higher production costs than their American competitors. In a free flow market I do not know how they are expected to overcome that difficulty. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is really curious. This took brains, for Canada is one of the few countries in the world that has been able cleverly to discriminate against its own domestic manufacturers. We should be proud of ourselves for dreaming up this arrangement. We would hope the government would give consideration to removing this tax. This matter has been raised on many occasions, but again I think we got the blind eye on it, although I am not quite sure.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, my time is running out and in conclusion I should like to make a couple of observations concerning certain features of
May 5, 1966	COMMONS
the agreement which worry us. I know it will be approved. In fact I think the minister would have to commit suicide if by some miracle we did not approve it. What would he do, if by any strange chance we turned down an agreement which has been in effect for 15 months. This agreement confirms, once and for all, the complete domination of our automotive industry by United States subsidiaries. A large United States owned auto producer has a tremendous advantage in this kind of nationalized market which you are bringing about. If ever there was any doubt about it, it now is settled for all time that our industry is completely dominated by the United States subsidiaries in this field.
Second, the pact is one sided, mostly in favour of Canada, and perhaps we should congratulate the minister on good horse trading in that regard. In any event, it is dependent on the benevolent good will of the United States auto companies. This is the first time, in my knowledge, where a Canadian government policy is subject to the whims and good will of American private business. It will be interesting to watch 1968, when this comes up again, because by that time the integration will be so complete that there never will be any opportunity to reverse it; that may be inevitable, but at least it is established.
Third, this constitutes a disturbing integration of our facilities with those of the United States. It makes us, therefore, highly vulnerable to United States decisions. This too may be inevitable, but it now is pretty obvious that from here on in the decisions we can make in one of the greatest industries we have are not our own to make. They will be very vulnerable in respect of decisions from Washington or Detroit. Indeed, from now on when Washington hiccups Ottawa will tremble in the automobile business.
Fourth, this represents a strange paradox in government thinking-a subsidy of many millions of dollars and a tax on building materials for the houses our people have to provide. There is something wrong in this approach. Maybe we will sort it out before the debate is over.
Fifth, there has been disturbing talk, not from the minister but by some of the responsible backbenchers, of an extension of this type of development into other areas. We have heard of tires, forest products, and an extension of this whole plan to other sectors of the economy. I hope this is not so, and I hope the government will go very carefully.

The automobile industry is unique; there is nothing like it in North America. We have a few large foreign owned firms producing the same products on both sides of the border. To extend this would continue the integration of Canada with the United States and, just as important, it would create great harm for Canadian firms operating in an industry which is not United States owned, because they would be at a fantastic disadvantage, one which they could not overcome.
When speaking of integration with the United States, most of us feel this government is committed, in that they have accepted the view that we have passed the point of no return and that it will be a lot easier in the long run to integrate smoothly with the United States economy. I think the continen-talists have taken over in this government, notwithstanding the window dressing, and that they really have accepted the fact that it is too late and we cannot overcome this American ownership.
Those are the problems in this agreement. We realize we cannot stop it nor, perhaps, would we. These are the disturbing aspects of it about which I would hope the minister would try to set our minds at ease before we rubberstamp it.
May I say one further word. The minister is interested in auto safety. We hear in the press that he is preparing a voluntary code of auto safety to be issued shortly. I should like to suggest to him that if he really is serious about auto safety, he should remenber his experience with the voluntary participation of the companies under this legislation, and if their participation in auto safety is as good as it has been under this, it is useless to be designing and issuing the code.
Briefly those are our suggestions, and they will be enlarged upon by other members of my party as the debate proceeds.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate briefly in the debate on the auto agreement because in my constituency of Halton is one of the largest auto manufacturers, the Ford Motor Company of Canada. If we look back to the minister's statement on the introduction of this trade agreement, we will see that the statement said it was a program designed to achieve a substantial expansion in production and employment, and to promote improved competitive efficiency in this important sector of Canadian manufacturing.
4768	COMMONS
Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement
I think everyone in this house will agree that the automobile manufacturing industry is one of the backbones of Canadian industry. This pact will give the Canadian automobile industry free access to the huge United States, or really the huge North American market. What we really are hoping to accomplish in this agreement are three things primarily: first of all, increased production and a larger share of the North American market; second, increased employment in Canada; third, to improve competitive efficiency as reflected in the cost of automobiles to the automobile buyer.
I think, because the program has been in effect since January 1965, we now at this time can decide whether this to date has been a successful program. Under the first heading, increased production, we have, or have plans for, 69 new plants, and 136 plants which are planning expansions. The value of the capital investment in Canada in respect of these new plants to be constructed is $400 million approximately, and for those which will expand their facilities an investment in Canada of capital of more than $335 million.
In the Toronto-Hamilton area, which is relatively well within the reach of my constituency, we have 25 new plants, and 38 which are expanding their facilities, a total of 63 plants with a capital investment of something in the neighbourhood of $75 million. As was mentioned earlier, there is no question but that the production of commercial vehicles in Canada has been rising steadily. As an example, in 1965 our production was up approximately 28 per cent from 1964. Reference already has been made to export and import of cars. Car parts and accessories, both exports and imports, are up. I think it is encouraging to all of us to know that the rate of increase of exports is greater than the rate of increase of imports. We certainly hope those two lines would meet.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The second factor, increased employment, has truly come about. There were approximately 57,000 people employed in the automobile industries in Canada in 1963; there were 66,000 in 1964 and 77,000 in 1965. I am pleased that approximately 1,700 additional workers have been employed in the automobile industry in the Toronto and Hamilton area of my riding, and that in the entire industry, as the minister mentioned earlier, there are something in the neighbourhood of 10,000 new jobs which have been
[Mr. Harley.l

created, with a potential addition of 7,000 in the foreseeable future.
Several members have already made reference to the comparative costs of automobiles. We have been pleased to note in the last car price list for 1966 models that there has been a narrowing of the gap between the United States and Canadian prices. We expect and hope that this trend will continue until there is equality in these prices.
It would appear that as a result of the conditions laid down at the time of the introduction of this automobile agreement we have been very successful. The things we hoped would be accomplished by this agreement appear to have been partially accomplished and I am sure that this trend will continue. Let me illustrate this success by reference to certain things which have happened in my riding.
In 1964 the construction of a $25 million truck plant commenced. Recently it was officially opened. An additional shift has been instituted at that plant and at this time 400 trucks per day, through a two-shift program, are being produced. It is interesting to note that this truck plant is designed to produce as many trucks per year as were sold in 1965 by the entire Canadian industry.
This year the Ford Motor Company announced another $13 million program to modify and re-equip a passenger car assembly plant in the Oakville area. As we are all aware, other changes are taking place at Windsor and Talbotville, to which reference will be made by other speakers. These facts reflect the boom which is taking place in this area, with attendant improvements to all sectors of the economy.
The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) referred to the closure of the purchasing department of the Ford Motor Company at Oakville. I should like to elaborate on that reference and point out that a portion of the purchasing department has remained in Oakville, while part of its operations have moved to Windsor and part to Dearborn, Michigan. It is my understanding this change was contemplated long before the automotive agreement came into effect. While the signing of the agreement may have advanced this move, it was one that was due to take place in any event. As a member of parliament for that area I received only one telephone call in protest of this change. To my knowledge the employees transferred were given equal or better job opportunities. The

company did not force these employees to move, but allowed them to remain in Canada at Oakville, if they so desired.
I feel very strongly that this automobile agreement has been advantageous to Canada. Unlike the hon. member who just resumed his seat, I feel the government should consider implementation of similar agreements in respect of other industries, provided safeguards are included to protect Canadian industry. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) suggested a few minutes ago that the government has taken what is popularly termed as the continentalists' view, and that it was its ultimate intention to extend this type of agreement to other industries operating in the two countries. This article in part states:
Speaking at the annual meeting of the Oxford Liberal association, Mr. Laing said that to achieve this end, Canada would continue to strive for lower tariffs and would trade with any country in the world in all but strategic items.
That is a very interesting statement. The article begins by stating:
Arthur Laing, federal minister of northern affairs and natural resources, yesterday said that the ultimate goal of Liberalism in Canada is free trade.
That may be the government's policy, but I think it is something that should be watched carefully by everyone, particularly by the opposition parties in this house.
I do not think many members of this house oppose this auto parts treaty as such, but as was pointed out by the hon. member for Danforth, the automobile industry in North America is a very unique operation, probably not duplicated anywhere else in the world. For that reason, special considerations and regulations must be applied. It is to be hoped

had a succession of ministers visiting us trying to explain what a great thing the auto parts treaty is for this country. First of all the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) visited us last year and read a very interesting prepared speech, although he did not seem prepared at that time to answer any questions on it. Recently the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) visited us and told us what a great thing the automotive parts treaty is. The Minister of Industry himself was in my area during the last election explaining briefly what a good thing the treaty is. The former minister of mines and technical surveys was down there too. There are a number of other items which I could mention at this time, but these have been covered by other members, the member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) and the member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), and I see no point in repetition. However, there is one thing I would like to say to the minister, and I hope he can see his way clear to agree to this. While it is true that a number of representations have been made to the government pointing out the difficulties which a number of firms are encountering in this regard, I would hope that the minister would see fit to refer this treaty to the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy Development, because I believe that is the committee that would be concerned. The automotive parts industry and related industries in this country from which

I would very much hope that the minister would give consideration to referring this treaty to a committee. In conclusion I have but one other brief observation. It was pointed out by the minister in his early remarks that one of the hopes of the treaty was that Canadian auto parts manufacturers would have an opportunity to compete in the United States market-not only in the United States market but in the continental market as a whole. I believe that this is a most commendable idea. However, as I mentioned briefly a few moments ago, and I would like to reiterate it at this point, this is simply not working out. The large automobile companies, and again I mention particularly the Chrysler Corporation and the Ford Motor Company, have large numbers of wholly owned subsidiaries in the United States. I have been informed that when very efficient Canadian auto parts manufacturers-and I refer to the Ingersoll Machine and Tool Company, for one-have requested an opportunity to tender on some of the auto parts for these large companies, they were simply told: You cannot even tender on these contracts; we have our wholly owned subsidiaries in the United States, so why should we allow any other firm to offer tenders because we will get them from our wholly owned subsidiaries.

I am sure this is something the minister and the officials did not envisage at the time the treaty was signed. They may well have had assurances from these automobile companies that this would not take place. However, this is what has taken place. It can be called an Otto proposal under which this agreement can be enlarged. I believe it is no mystery to the minister and to all of us, that every country in the world wants to export manufactured goods; no country in the world wants to export raw materials. We also know that it is not possible for every country to export more manufactured goods than they import. If the hon. gentleman from Danforth was very worried about the word "continentalist", I am not at all worried about this as long as it means that each individual in each country can get a product produced most efficiently regardless of where it is produced, and as long as there is an equitable balance of trade.
This agreement could be interpreted as the first break in the old line of thinking where each country wanted to export more than it imported. I believe this agreement in reality wants to set an equitable basis; in other words it says: We shall export an amount equal to that we import. Now let us break this down. After all, this is free trade. The

Liberals have always been proponents of free trade. We want to break down the tariff. On the other hand we want it done in such a way that we in Canada can take advantage of our productive capacity.
What is this agreement in essence? I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say it means this, that in the automotive trade we have recognized that the salary scale and skills required are just about equal throughout the trade. We want to recognize the fact that in the United States, for example, automatic transmissions can be manufactured more efficiently than they can for the Canadian market. In other words, by the time you set up equipment and set up an assembly line, it is cheaper if you can manufacture 10 million items rather than one million.
In Canada we may be able to manufacture car bumpers more cheaply and efficiently, because plating requires electric power and we have the raw materials, the chrome, nickel and so on. Let us presume the skills required, the wages paid, and so on, in manufacturing those bumpers were the same as those in manufacturing transmissions. Would it not be feasible to allow United States companies to export to Canada $1 million worth of transmissions, provided we exported to the United States $1 million worth of car bumpers, or headlights, or anything which we manufacture better and more efficiently? That is the essence of this agreement and it is really the essence of free trade.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
However, if the manufacturers of transmissions used, let us say, $1 million worth of labour at $3 an hour and the bumper manufacturers used $1 million worth of labour at $1 an hour, the trade would not be equitable. The purpose of this agreement and its very content, as the minister explained, is much more equitable, because in the car industry-and this is probably why it was left in the car industry-the wage scale is almost identical.
Let us suppose the United States manufacturers say to us: We will export to Canada $1 million worth of transmissions, but we do not want anything else except $1 worth of farm machinery. What is wrong with that? The skills required in the manufacturing of farm machinery and the wage scales are identical to those in the automotive trade. I say that this would also be acceptable.
May 5, 19S6

To go a step further, supposing a United States manufacturer says: "I will export into Canada tariff-free $1 million worth of transmissions and will import from Canada $1 million worth of furniture"-or carved wood, which Canadians can produce much more efficiently, and where the scale of wages and the skills required are also identical, or possibly even higher. There is nothing wrong with that at all. In other words, we have already established the principle of a balance of trade, not in dollar volume but in manpower, man-hours requiring identical skills and more or less the same wages.
You can understand, Mr. Speaker, that it would be possible under the present system of balance of trade for Canada to export to the United States $5 billion worth of gas reserves, oil, electric power, fresh water resources, and many other items of natural resources which may not require the employment of very many people. At the same time, does this mean that we can import into Canada sewing machines, radios, television sets, cars and so on? No. But that is the basis on which we have worked up till now-a balance of trade based on dollar volume, which is fallacious and is not really a balance of trade. That is where we find ourselves in difficulty. What we have been doing is hypothecating our natural resources in exchange for manufactured goods. But this agreement puts a new emphasis on a balance of trade in man-hours and skills rather than on dollar volume.
There is some talk about extending this agreement to, or making a new agreement with, the timber and lumber business. We can also do it in the plastics business, the chemicals industry and the services industry. We might find ourselves with 1,000 agreements with United States manufacturers.
In other words, I am saying we must formulate now, general policies which include the essence of the automotive trade agreement and put the trade agreement on a wide, general basis. There has been since 1959 a movement toward a export-import parity program. I have been a manufacturer, an exporter and an importer. I can see the difficulty in all these enterprises. The export-import parity program which I have promoted for many years is more general than the automotive trade agreement but is on exactly the same lines-to balance our imports and exports according to man-hours, skills and salary schedules rather than dollar volume.
Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement
Some economists have said for years that it really does not matter whether we sell $20 million worth of gas reserves and import $20 million worth of radios and television sets; it is the same thing. Their argument is that $20 million received for gas reserves would be spent in Canada on the purchase of consumer goods, and so on. That is not so, first of all because $15 million of that $20 million automatically goes to the United States because the United States owns 75 per cent of the gas reserve companies. This leaves $5 million, out of which comes profit and promotion, with little remaining. So that the argument the economists put forward, that it does not really matter as long as money is exchanged for something, really does not hold water.
Although we are talking about the automotive trade agreement-and the exact program could be extended to other agreements-I should like to put forward the proposition that, by and large, tariffs are really a punitive measure. That is to say, they penalize an importer for importing goods and do not give any incentive to an exporter.
For example, let us say I am a manufacturer of air conditioning parts, as I have been, and let us suppose that the tariff regulations were changed and the essence of this agreement was enlarged. If I exported $1,000 worth of air conditioning equipment to the United States or elsewhere, and supposing, Mr. Speaker, I then received a permit to import $1,000 worth of goods of the same category-say, sewing machines or radios, which are in the same category as air conditioners-free of tariff. In other words, I have exported $1,000 worth of man hours in the production of a certain category of goods and I now have the right to import goods of like nature free of tariff. That is not a punitive measure at all.
Let us suppose I do not want to import anything, but was allowed to put this import permit on the market and somebody gave me $200, which is 20 per cent of the $1,000. I can reduce my costs in this way because really I receive $1,200 for the exports, and the person importing other goods has had to pay the $200 difference. But he has not paid it to the government as a punitive measure; he has paid it to the exporter. In this way an importer pays an incentive to the exporter.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We could also have the different categories related to each other. Let us suppose that I did not have a permit for goods in category
May 5, 1966

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement "C", but there was available $5,000 worth of goods in category "A", such as farm products, for example, which were still relatively balanced with the different products in category "C" and the amount of money paid to produce them, the skills required, and the wage schedule involved.
We have to get away from the punitive measure of tariffs and enlarge this automotive agreement, not industry for industry but on general principle. If my proposal were followed, you would really have no tariff at all; instead you would have an incentive. Or, the tariff which would normally be paid to the government would be paid to the exporter as a further incentive, and in time all this would balance itself out. No one in GATT or anyone else would blame us. We do not want to take advantage of anyone. We only want to make the same kind of things as others, and we want to export and import products, not in dollar value, but in terms of manhours and skills. We want to be equitable with others; we do not want to take advantage of anybody. The only way we can ensure a proper use of our natural resources is to produce those things that our training, and resources and abilities fit us for, and to import those things which can be produced better elswhere.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I believe that this agreement is the first step. It is a good step. I have no doubt that in time there will be other measures such as this one, in connection with other industries. However, we cannot have 1,000 or 10,000 agreements for different industries. We must have one general authority. We must maintain the principle that the Liberal government has always followed, of striving toward free trade, but equitable free trade. The only way that this can be done is to try to plan our imports and exports, not in terms of dollar value, not in terms of natural resources in exchange for manufactured products, but in terms of man-hours and the skills which are necessary to produce these things.
I entirely favour this agreement. I know that the reaction to it will be good, so far as Canada is concerned. I think that the idea behind this measure can be enlarged to include other industries, so that in time we shall have a general policy in connection with a new concept in trade balance.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking about this agreement


not as a member whose constituency is affected in so far as employment therein is concerned, but because I want to take a look at this particular automobile agreement from a long range point of view.
I must say that I find it very regrettable that there has been this delay of almost 15 months in bringing the agreement before parliament. I need not repeat what was said by the hon. member for Wellington South and by the hon. member for Danforth with regard to the great secrecy under which this agreement was signed. It was said that the minister did not want to disclose information about it because negotiations were going on. At one time it was anticipated that this agreement might be considered by parliament last fall. Of course our calculations were put out by having an unnecessary election, and this measure was one of the casualties of that ill-fated sortie.
Now, 15 months after its inception, the government is asking this house to rubber-stamp the agreement. This is what is thoroughly repugnant to me. We are asked to rubberstamp this agreement, with the plea that if this house would have turned it down, scores of industrialists and thousands of workers would have been prejudiced, because they relied on the steps taken under the agreement which were taken prior to ratification by parliament. This is a form of not-so-subtle blackmail on this house. The house is being blackjacked to accept this agreement. As a principle, I find that to be wrong, regardless of the terms of the agreement, whether they be good, bad or indifferent.
What I object to thoroughly is the timing of the government, and the delay in bringing this agreement before parliament. It was not necessary to delay it. This should have been considered last June. However, other things crept in that were not necessary.
Having said that, I do not want to go over points made by other hon. members in the house respecting labour dislocation, respecting the cross-purposes that the government is working at by the maintenance of sales tax on production machinery, and by the maintenance of import duties on that machinery. In fact, in so far as buying the machinery is concerned, we are paying more for it as a result of the altered position of the dollar, for which the government is not responsible. But this is what our manufacturers are facing. When we say that we are going to have some sort of rapprochement or parity of costs and of prices for automobiles in this country, we
May 5, 1966	COMMONS
are frankly deluding ourselves. This will be so until Canadian manufacturers can be in the position of their United States counterparts who do not have to pay the silly 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery, or the import duty on machinery.
Next we are going to hear about the parity of wages as between American and Canadian automobile workers, regardless of whether production per man hour is going to be equivalent on both sides of the border. That makes no difference to those advocating this parity, who just look at the dollar sign, and who do not look at what is done to earn that dollar. If this parity begins in the automobile industry, and this is expected, the next step will be to bring it into the steel industry and to related industries, one after the other.
Where do we go from there, so far as Canadian industrial production is concerned?
I would suggest, by introducing the measure under consideration, that we, as Canadians, have embarked on a very dangerous toboggan slide, and we may be in a position where we have to go along for the ride, to the bottom of the slope, unable to control our course.
These are some of the questions that have to be examined. They have not been discussed in the house. They have not been exposed by the minister. He has not spoken about this question of parity wages. He has not spoken about the suggestions being put forward by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) and by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley).
Similar types of agreements might be contemplated to be entered into in other industries. I should like to hear from the Minister of Industry about some of these kites that his colleagues are flying. I do not agree with the minister's thinking. I have some grave reservations as to this agreement because of the penury of information. The minister quoted statistics. He gave, in percentages, increases of exports and increases of imports. If my memory serves me correctly, the financial pages of the newspapers within the last fortnight have indicated that the increases of imports on a dollar basis exceed the increases of exports on a dollar basis.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The position is no better. As a matter of fact, it is worse, from the position of the balance of payments. Where has been the gain? After all, this auto agreement was designed to deal specifically with the evergrowing deficit on international account. The

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement minister may shake his head but there are many people who will disagree with him. It would be a valid reason. Remember, we are facing a deficit which amounts to roughly $600 million on the automobile account each year. It would be well worth striving for, to reduce a deficit of these proportions. If the present agreement has the result of reducing the deficit on the commodity account with the United States, let us give three cheers. That would be a point in its favour. But so far this has not been the case. The gap has widened. What will it be next year? Will the gap be wider still?
The minister spoke about increases in production but these increases are not attributable to the agreement-not all of them, by any means. The Canadian public has itself been responsible for a good deal of the increase in sales, whether the increase is measured in units of 100,000 vehicles, or in percentages or in dollars. The Canadian public has bought more vehicles. It is true that somewhere along the line we may have shared in an increase in the consumption in the United States. But let us not seek to give the impression that all this increase has suddenly come about because an auto agreement was made. To do so would, in the best possible light, amount to innocent misrepresentation and in another light it could amount to deliberate misrepresentation of the facts. As I say, I am not satisfied with the information we have been given with regard to this agreement. Neither is anyone else in this house.
I ask a further question. What is the value of this automotive agreement to those regions in Canada where there are no parts manufacturers or assembly plants and where the work force is not directly affected? Ministers went around the country last fall, receiving appropriate publicity-pieces were put in various newspapers by inspired writers-all announcing with great fanfare that the public would see a reduction in prices as a result of this pact. There was to be a substantial narrowing of the gap between the prices of a particular model in Canada and in the United States. We all know what happened last fall when the price increases were announced. The manufacturers suggested they were price reductions.
I believe it was the Chrysler Corporation which made the first announcement of a price increase. It did not meet with the approval of the United States administration and serious growling came out of Washington. The next company to do the same thing-I believe it
May 5, 1966

Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement was Ford-followed a different approach using the soft sell. They indicated that a number of formerly optional so-called safety features were being added and that the price was therefore being advanced slightly.
As it turned out, the increase in price substantially exceeded the increase in the cost of those particular features. On all those cars the company was picking up an extra amount between $25 and $50. The next step was a parallel announcement in Canada-that there was a reduction in price. But the movement in both countries was in the same direction. There was no narrowing of the gap.
